On real indoor RSS measurements from 52 transmitter locations, Gaussian filtering raises PCD accuracy from 0.870 to 0.921 when the PCD is trained on 10 locations and from 0.905 to 0.925 when trained on 40. On synthetic attack and no-attack sequences built from the same measurements, evaluated on a held-out test set of 1,679 sequences, the best classifier (XGBoost) reaches an accuracy of 0.949 and an F1 score of 0.940, and random forests reach an AUC of 0.99. The detector separates static attackers almost perfectly but misses about a third of attacks in which two transmitters move simultaneously, which produce region sequences similar to those of a single moving user.

papers.title: Graded version of local-global principle for Steinberg and Chevalley groups
papers.abstract: In this article, an analog of a graded version of Quillen-Suslin's local-global principle was established for Steinberg groups $St(Φ,-)$ and Chevalley groups $G(Φ,-)$ over a reduced irreducible root system $Φ$.

papers.title: Zero-sum subsequences of cross number $1$ over cyclic groups
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, and let $\mathsf{T}(G)$ be the smallest integer $t$ such that every sequence of length $t$ over $G$ contains a nonempty zero-sum subsequence of cross number $1$. We determine the exact value of $\mathsf{T}(C_n)$ for every positive integer $n$, showing that $\mathsf{T}(C_n)=2n-1$ when $n$ is odd and $\mathsf{T}(C_n)=3n/2-1$ when $n$ is even. In particular, $\mathsf{T}(C_n)=\mathsf{s}(C_n)$ for odd $n$.

papers.title: Match Rate Is Not Match Quality
papers.abstract: Third-party identity-resolution vendors commonly emphasize match rate, the share of submitted records they can link to identifiers for advertising activation, as their core metric of quality. Yet a high match rate does not necessarily mean that those matched identifiers belong to the submitted records (i.e., the intended targets). In this paper we explore match quality as an alternative metric to match rate, utilizing a unique data set to evaluate match quality. We are able to compare two demographics, age and gender, from a submitted record (voter files) to the same demographics in self-reported surveys matched to mobile advertising identifiers linked together by two leading identity-resolution vendors. The data and matching was from 2019-20. There is substantial ambiguity in match quality of the returned records. First, both vendors' activation files contain multiple device identifiers per match. Second, match quality among audited pairs (Vendor A) and for explicitly labeled individual-level matches (Vendor B) is only 21.8% and 23.6%, respectively. Utilizing a mixture model that assumes that correct links always agree on these two demographics and incorrect links agree 10% of the time, these rates imply conditional identity-level precisions of approximately 15% and 13%, respectively. This paper utilizes identity-resolution products that are several years old, but the question we address remains fundamental: match rate alone cannot establish whether advertisers are reaching the people they intended. Evaluating identity resolution requires independent evidence of match quality alongside match rate.

papers.title: Pseudocompact MAD families under $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak c$
papers.abstract: We prove that if the bounding number $\mathfrak b$ equals the cardinality of the continuum $\mathfrak c$, then every infinite almost disjoint family of size less than $\mathfrak c$ can be extended to a maximal almost disjoint family whose Isbell--Mrówka space has a pseudocompact Vietoris hyperspace.

papers.title: Zippers and Twisters II: The lopsidedness of satellite systems around local massive galaxies emerges from a shifting cosmic web landscape
papers.abstract: We investigate the role of the cosmic web on the origin and strength of lopsidedness in the distributions of luminous dwarf satellites around massive galaxies analogs in the high-resolution hydrodynamic simulation NewHorizon. Using common lopsidedness estimators, we find that $>25\%$ of our sample display ``statistically significant" lopsidedness incompatible with expectations for dark matter sub-haloes. The NewHorizon sample is generally skewed towards being more lopsided than naive expectations. This cautions against using dark matter or under-resolved hydrodynamic simulations as a null-hypothesis to compare to real systems. We find broad, hemispheric lopsidedness to be much more prevalent than narrow lopsidedness inherited from group infall. Across all systems, the dividing plane between the richest and emptiest hemispheres is systematically aligned with a nearby intermediate-scale cosmic filament. Further analysis reveals that the lopsidedness of systems is largely inherited from that of the network of filaments feeding them. The most populated side almost systematically contains the highest number of filaments. Such anisotropies of local filament networks are often indicative of on-going or recent zippers (filament merger $<2$ Gyr). Converging filamentary structures therefore funnel satellites preferentially onto one side of host halos, naturally generating lopsided configurations without requiring galaxy mergers. Twister remnants (of high orbital momentum mergers of filaments) are also found on the richest hemisphere of our systems, perhaps reminiscent of vorticity preventing mergers hence causing satellites' pooling. These results suggest that lopsidedness is primarily an outcome of the evolution of the intermediate-scale cosmic web. This highlights the need for increased hydrodynamic resolution in simulations.

papers.title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
papers.abstract: Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations. We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at https://github.com/AMDResearch/kiwi.

papers.title: Great Listeners, Poor Decision-Makers: Rethinking Agentic Audio AI
papers.abstract: Audio artificial intelligence (AI) now recognizes speech, sounds, and music remarkably well, yet voice agents still act when they should not: they execute commands addressed to others, act on misheard content, and commit before the user finishes speaking. This position article argues that the bottleneck in agentic audio AI has shifted from recognition to decision-making. We propose a reference architecture with an explicit decision layer, separate from perception and reasoning, that chooses whether to act, wait, ask, or remain silent from evidence on addressedness, speaker identity, content confidence, tool reliability, utterance completeness, and action risk. We motivate the design through six recurring decision failures and a decision-theoretic argument that transcript confidence alone is insufficient to justify an action. We implement the layer with fuzzy inference, evolutionary optimization, and sequential decision-making, and evaluate it through simulations, ablations, and recorded audio, including egocentric recordings. Addressedness and speaker evidence matter most, risk-aware gating suppresses costly errors, and well-tuned policies perform similarly, with fuzzy gates more robust to overconfident addressedness estimates. On recorded audio, explicit gating cuts executed side talk from 41\% to 7--10\% while serving 83--85\% of valid requests under successful clarification, outperforming prompting-based baselines. These results support explicit action gating as an architectural requirement for reliable voice agents.

papers.title: Defining equations for two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties
papers.abstract: We give a complete algebraic characterization of two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties. We show that the determinantal equations arising from rank constraints imposed by the activation patterns generate the defining ideals, thereby proving a conjecture of Alexandr-Montúfar. The set-theoretic proof uses a characterization of orbit closures of matrix pencils in terms of the Kronecker canonical form.

papers.title: ReflectScene:MLLM-Guided Closed-Loop Diffusion for 3D Indoor Scene Generation
papers.abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence.We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising.Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.

papers.title: Weighing the Envelope: Component Weight and Arbitration in Envelope-Layer Defenses for a Single LLM Agent
papers.abstract: The envelope layer is the channel through which malicious content enters an LLM agent. Prior work established label and memory effects on multi-agent A2A envelopes, but the weight structure when MCP tools and memory coexist in a single agent remains unclear. Our threat model assumes an attacker pre-plants a malicious tool and poisons long-term memory; a benign user request inadvertently triggers it, and the attacker never enters the conversation. Following GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D, we measure how labels, memory, tool roles, and the backend shape invocation decisions across label-memory conflict, tool roles, robustness, and tool generalization. A tool-side forced-verification label substantially reduces semantic breach, but strong success memory pulls it back; a memory-side downgrade statement returns the outcome to the level of the label alone. The label works through mandatory implementation inspection plus default denial, not length or format; memory authorization wording erodes it with dose, while position and multi-turn pressure do not change the defense direction. Tool roles divide label effects into substitution, suppression, and boundary failure: low penetration is not safety, local leakage is the main residual risk, and a second malicious tool shows the same direction. Envelope labels are not a switch but a measurable, reversible weight constrained by backend and tool role, acting as a soft gate and risk signal within a broader defense rather than a substitute for permissions, sandboxing, or human review.

papers.title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

papers.title: Implementation of LDA+Gutzwiller with Newton's method
papers.abstract: In order to calculate the electronic structure of correlated materials, we propose implementation of the LDA+Gutzwiller method with Newton's method. The self-consistence process, efficiency and convergence of calculation are improved dramatically by using Newton's method with golden section search and other improvement approaches. We compare the calculated results by applying the previous linear mix method and Newton's method. We have applied our code to study the electronic structure of several typical strong correlated materials, including SrVO$_3$, LaCoO$_3$, and La$_2$O$_3$Fe$_2$Se$_2$. Our results fit quite well with the previous studies.

papers.title: Capability Internet: A Network Architecture for Autonomous Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly provide and consume network services. An agent coordinating a long-running task across organizations must track what has been done, which actions are authorized, and which provider can perform the next step. We propose Capability Internet (CI), an architecture in which agents exchange capabilities and coordinate their use through persistent tasks. Versioned descriptions specify behavior, and live instances identify the providers and resources that can supply it. Task records link each invocation to its selected instance, authority, and terms of use. When providers change, the task can reuse completed results that still meet its requirements. Five functions support capability discovery, task coordination, federated compute, intelligence reuse, and governance of capability use and settlement. Reviewed task results can supply versioned intelligence for subsequent tasks. We illustrate CI through four deployment profiles covering computing and intelligence services, manufacturing, vehicles and embodied robots, and space-ground operations, and propose an evaluation plan.

papers.title: TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery
papers.abstract: Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.

papers.title: Re-Testing LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translations Against Their Original C
papers.abstract: Most C-to-Rust translators use large language models (LLMs), and each reports a success rate from its own correctness check. We survey 34 C-to-Rust translators that use LLMs. Only one reports testing its check, and eleven release the original C and their Rust in runnable form. We re-test all eleven. We run the C and the Rust on generated inputs, compare every output, and count a divergence only where the C has no undefined behavior. All eleven release defective translations: we find 160 defects, 93 of them outright errors on ordinary inputs. Their own checks accepted 86 defective translations. For 81 of them, the released check never compared the programs on an input that exposes the defect. For three of the other five, it ran one but compared only part of the output. A success rate is only as good as its check. Before counting a translation as a success, authors should compare every output with the C's on inputs the repair loop never saw, check that a verifier reaches its assertion, release exactly what the check accepted, and report how they tested the check.

papers.title: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.

papers.title: Materials representations organize transferable supervision for chemical extrapolation
papers.abstract: Materials discovery often requires chemical extrapolation beyond labeled data. When target compounds contain elements absent from training, which compounds of other elements provide transferable supervision remains unclear. Here we show that, without target-property labels, materials representations rank other elements by the supervision their compounds provide. Engineered descriptors rank them largely by elemental-property similarity, whereas a pretrained crystal-graph encoder ranks them by the geometry of its learned representation. At fixed training-set size, excluding the compounds of the encoder's six top-ranked elements raises formation-energy and bandgap errors by 100-110 meV per atom and 42-85 meV, versus little change for six lower-ranked elements. The rankings hold across properties, regressors and datasets. The encoder's ranking outperforms elemental-property similarity and periodic groups, suggesting that it captures how elements behave within compounds. Materials representations thus organize transferable supervision, which can be identified before model training, informing dataset assessment and label acquisition.

papers.title: Online State-Representation Adaptation under Synthetic Interaction-Cue Remapping
papers.abstract: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.

papers.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

papers.title: Unpolarized Generalized Parton Distributions of the Nucleon in a Covariant Quark-Diquark Approach
papers.abstract: We study the unpolarized generalized parton distributions (GPDs) of the nucleon in a covariant quark-diquark approach, in which both scalar and axial-vector diquarks are treated as composite subsystems. Motivated by previous form factor studies, we introduce a vertex correction based on the pion cloud picture as a first exploratory treatment of pion cloud effects at the GPD level, in order to improve the description of $E^q(ξ, x, t)$ and related magnetic observables. At the model input scale, only valence quarks are included. With the vertex correction, the electromagnetic form factors $G_{E, M}$ and the mass form factor $A$ obtained from the Mellin moments of the GPDs agree well with those obtained from direct calculations. The vertex correction brings the evolved charge weighted distribution $\sum{e^q E^q(ξ, x, t)}$ closer to the phenomenological parametrization. The correction shifts transverse strength from the central region toward the peripheral region, consistent with the long range character of the pion cloud contribution. The transverse structure results further suggest a harder longitudinal momentum distribution in the central region of the nucleon than in its periphery. Furthermore, the evolved real part of the proton Compton form factor, $\mathrm{Re} \mathcal{H}(ξ, t)$, has a reasonable magnitude and follows the main trend of the Quantum Deep Neural Networks (QDNN) extraction. In addition, $\mathrm{Re} \mathcal{H}$ may be more sensitive to the ERBL region than the other physical quantities calculated in this work.

papers.title: Symplectic $\mathbb{CP}^n$ recognition and filling rigidity via Rabinowitz Floer homology
papers.abstract: We prove that a symplectic manifold $X$ admitting a pseudo-holomorphic line through two generic points, formulated as the non-vanishing of a genus zero Gromov--Witten invariant, is (rationally) homotopy equivalent to $\mathbb{CP}^n$, with identical first Chern class and quantum cohomology. Together with generalizations of this result to pseudo-holomorphic lines with tangency constraints, they provide a new mechanism for establishing the topological uniqueness of Liouville fillings of certain contact manifolds. We obtain filling rigidity for the ideal boundary of a class of affine varieties that admit $\mathbb{CP}^n$ as a compactification; notable examples include the ideal boundary of the complement of any hyperplane arrangement and $ST^*\mathbb{RP}^n$ for $n\ge 3$. The proofs are based on Rabinowitz Floer homology and its variants.

papers.title: A System 1 Decision Model for Medical Multiple-Choice Questions Built on Frozen Language Models
papers.abstract: A System 1 model answers a multiple-choice question in a single pass. A frozen language model turns the question and each option into vectors, two small, trained heads place them in a shared space, and the closest option wins. The design has been shown on agent decisions, but we are not aware of a study of how far it goes on exam questions that need medical knowledge, where the right option is often no more similar to the question than the wrong ones. We rebuilt the recipe from scratch for MedMCQA and trained only two projection heads and one temperature on top of frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, Granite-4.2-3B and Qwen3-8B, using a contrastive loss with in-batch and hard negatives and a mask for repeated answers. With plain last-token vectors, both small encoders answer about one question in three correctly (33.1% and 33.0% on 3,842 held-out questions, where chance is 25.0%). Writing each text inside a one-word-summary prompt and lowering the learning rate of the heads raised this to 41.7% and 42.5% for the two small encoders and to 46.0% +-0.2 (three seeds) for Qwen3-8B. Shuffling the questions against the options returns accuracy to chance, so the heads do use the question. Flan-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2 report 57.6% and 72.3% on MedMCQA under a different protocol, so ours is a cheap, fast baseline and not a competitive system. We also say what our evidence cannot show: validation gains were about 1.7 to 2 times the test gains, and we could not separate the effect of reading several encoder layers from the other changes.

papers.title: Bernstein-Zelevinsky duality for equivariant vector bundles on Drinfeld spaces
papers.abstract: We study duality and finiteness of locally analytic representations arising from compactly supported coherent cohomology of Drinfeld spaces. We prove that Grothendieck--Serre duality for equivariant vector bundles realizes Bernstein--Zelevinsky duality of locally analytic representations. We follow the strategy of Fargues for $\ell$-adic sheaves and obtain resolutions of locally analytic representations by compactly induced representations. The resolutions motivate us to introduce the notion of locally analytic representations of compact presentation, which generalizes the notion of finitely presented representations. These representations are related to prim objects on the classifying stack in the sense of $6$-functor formalism and their extension groups to admissible locally analytic representations are finite-dimensional. As an application, we establish Serre duality for extension groups of locally analytic representations of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ attached to non-trianguline de Rham Galois representations under the $p$-adic local Langlands correspondence.

papers.title: Estimation-Aware Reachability
papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability computes the states from which a system can be kept safe under worst-case disturbances, but it assumes the state is known exactly, whereas real robots act on noisy estimates whose uncertainty evolves with their motion. We extend Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability to the robot's belief, estimate and uncertainty, treating unexpected measurements as a bounded adversary and enlarging the unsafe set by the current uncertainty, so that certified states are safe with a prescribed probability. The formulation is compatible with existing solvers. In simulation, the resulting safety filters nearly eliminate the collisions of certaintyequivalent HJ and are less conservative than equally safe uncertainty-padding baselines. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/HimanshuPaudel/Estimation-Aware-Reachability

papers.title: Near-optimal convergence of Widlund's method and numerical exploration of different implementations
papers.abstract: For linear systems arising from the discretization of certain classes of mathematical models, the splitting of the linear system into its Hermitian and skew-Hermitian parts has a physical meaning. If, in addition, the Hermitian part is positive definite, there exist Krylov subspace methods based on three-term recurrences where the Hermitian part is used as a preconditioner. Two such Krylov subspace methods are Widlund's method and Rapoport's method. In this paper we establish a ``near-optimal'' guarantee for the convergence of Widlund's method, showing that the overall convergence of Widlund's method is nearly as good as that of Rapoport's method. Specifically, we show that for every iteration $k$, there exists an iteration $j\leq k$ where the residual norm of Widlund's method is less than $\sqrt{k+1} $ times the residual norm of Rapoport's method at iteration $k$. This bound is sharp. We also provide a computational study on various implementations of Widlund's method in the exact and inexact cases, and show that certain implementations may stagnate while others do not, i.e., we look at the robustness of the different implementations. We recommend two implementations.

papers.title: Euler-Lagrange Equations Formulated in Terms of Angular Velocity
papers.abstract: We propose a novel variant of the Euler--Lagrange (EL) equation for rigid body rotation, explicitly formulated in terms of orientation parameters $\thh$ and angular velocity $\omm$. Variational analysis of the stationarity condition of the action integral for a Lagrangian in terms of $\thh$ and $\omm$ yields a modified EL formulation. For pure rotational motion, the proposed equation directly recovers equations of motion fully consistent with the classical Euler equations, bypassing explicit geometry-based torque analysis. Furthermore, the framework seamlessly accommodates coupled translational and rotational dynamics, as validated through a spring-suspended symmetrical top, exhibiting exact agreement with the Newton--Euler equations. We also identify an inherent discrepancy in the standard EL approach, demonstrating that applying a direct coordinate transformation $\dot\thh\mapsto\omm$ causes the resulting formulation to deviate from both the classical Euler equation and our proposed formulation. The proposed framework is expected to provide an intuitive, versatile modeling tool for spatial rigid body dynamics.

papers.title: Covering the Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and the Design Effect of a Measurement Setting
papers.abstract: Quantum state tomography and shadow-based estimation rely on measuring Pauli observables. An experiment does not measure them one at a time: it chooses a measurement setting that assigns one of the bases X, Y or Z to each qubit, and a single run in that setting yields estimates of every Pauli observable compatible with it. We say that the setting covers those observables. We determine how many random settings cover a prescribed fraction of all Pauli observables. As the number of settings grows exponentially with the number of qubits, the covered fraction has a sharp threshold at a growth rate of $3^{3/4}$ per qubit, set by the rate-distortion function of covering at zero distortion. We give an explicit expression for the number of settings needed to reach a target fraction, accurate up to a remainder that reduces to a small oscillation for many qubits, and show that random sampling is asymptotically optimal up to a factor of less than 1.69. Coverage does not determine what a setting contributes to an estimator. Observables covered by one setting are estimated from the same outcomes, so their estimates are correlated. We quantify this correlation through the design effect of a setting, which equals the squared Pauli expectation that the setting captures and depends on the target state. We derive its mean over settings in closed form for every state and show that it can be estimated without bias from the measurement data. In simulations on six qubits, measuring settings needs 7.6 to 38 times fewer circuit runs than measuring the same number of observables independently. At high coverage, fitting the outcome histograms instead of averaged estimates roughly halves the reconstruction error, mainly because the fit counts how many settings cover each observable. The correlation itself costs such a fit about a factor of two, and a larger design effect signals more to gain from modeling it.

papers.title: Slice Isolation-as-a-Service: An Isolation Mechanism to Proactively Defend Cross-Slice Attacks in 5G-Advanced and Beyond
papers.abstract: As cellular networks transition toward 5G-Advanced and Sixth Generation (6G) architectures, Network Slicing (NS) remains essential for multiplexing heterogeneous services over shared physical infrastructure. However, deploying critical Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communications (URLLC) alongside standard broadband introduces severe cross-slice vulnerabilities. The implicit assumption that logical slicing inherently guarantees security fails against data plane exploits, as shared User Plane Functions (UPFs) remain susceptible to resource starvation and protocol tunneling. To address this, we propose the Slice Isolation-as-a-Service framework, which treats topological data plane isolation as an on-demand, monetizable capability. We formulate the multi-UPF resource allocation problem as a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model to strictly enforce physical and virtual isolation boundaries based on tenant security tiers, minimizing provisioning costs and end-to-end latency. To validate the framework, we engineered a novel containerized Fifth Generation (5G) testbed integrating Free5GC with Nokia Containerlab. Empirical evaluations under active volumetric flooding and the recently discovered GTP-in-GTP reflection attacks reveal that shared and Virtualized Network Function (VNF)-only isolation fail catastrophically, suffering up to 30% packet loss and complete bandwidth starvation. Our results prove that MINLP-driven strict physical isolation successfully neutralizes cross-slice injection and preserves 99.999% reliability for mission-critical slices, confirming our isolation framework as a crucial proactive defense for next-generation core networks.

papers.title: Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games
papers.abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.

papers.title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

papers.title: Observation of Exact Mobility-Edge Phases in Two-Dimensional Photonic Quasicrystals
papers.abstract: Mobility edges, separating localized and extended states in energy, are central to localization physics. While exact mobility edges have been established in several one-dimensional quasiperiodic models, their realization in two dimensions remains largely unexplored. Here, we uncover a general route to exact mobility edges in the two-dimensional Aubry-Andre quasicrystal by introducing auxiliary subsystems. Through isospectral reduction, we reveal a hidden self-dual structure that yields exact mobility-edge conditions, separating extended, localized, and partially localized states in the spectrum. Tailoring the auxiliary structures controls the effective couplings and resulting mobility edge configurations, while auxiliary resonances further support flat-band states. In a decorated Lieb-type quasicrystal, we experimentally realize these predicted phases in photonic waveguide lattices and probe their energy-dependent localization through site-selective quench dynamics. Our results provide a versatile platform for controlling localization and can be readily extended to other physical platforms and higher-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Mapping the Design Space of Feature Sampling for Optical Flow
papers.abstract: The computation of correlation features is crucial for optical flow estimation. Existing methods (e.g., RAFT) perform fixed-radius lookups on a cost volume, yielding a set of correlation features for each position; alternatively, WAFT performs single-point feature indexing, yielding one correlation feature vector per position. None of them designs a suitable correlation feature sampling scheme for each position according to regional characteristics. Our insight is that not every position requires the same sampling scheme. Applying an identical sampling scheme to every position is either redundant or insufficient and ignores the specific characteristics of the corresponding region. This paper rethinks the design of feature sampling and investigates the following question: should the support of feature sampling---i.e., the extent and directions over which evidence is aggregated---be learned separately for each query position? To study this question, we propose SAGE (Sampling with Anisotropic Gaussian Expectation). This method replaces single-point sampling with a per-pixel anisotropic Gaussian expectation on a fixed candidate grid centered on the current optical flow estimate. A positive-definite precision matrix controls the scale, anisotropy, and orientation of the sampling support, with single-point sampling included as its limiting case. Consequently, the sampling support becomes an explicit and analyzable design variable and provides a principled way to analyze how directional feature aggregation affects correspondence learning. Extensive experiments show that SAGE, while adding only 1.5% multiply-accumulate operations (MACs), effectively improves zero-shot cross-dataset generalization. When trained only on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings, SAGE reduces the end-point error (EPE) by 24.2% and 16.4% on Sintel clean and final, and reduces KITTI F1-epe and F1-all by 7.2% and 11.6%.

papers.title: Hurwitz equivalence in quandles of order at most four
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a quandle and let $m\geq 2$ be an integer. The $m$-braid group acts on the $m$-fold Cartesian power $X^m$ by the Hurwitz action. For an $m$-tuple $\boldsymbol{x}\in X^m$, we introduce two invariants of the Hurwitz action: the product $Π(\boldsymbol{x})$ of its entries in the associated group $\operatorname{As}(X)$ and the orbit multiplicities $μ_w(\boldsymbol{x})$ $(w\in X)$. We prove that these two invariants completely classify Hurwitz equivalence classes for all quandles of order at most four. We also establish a complete classification of Hurwitz equivalence classes for a class of amalgamated sums of trivial quandles and a reduction theorem for disjoint sums with trivial quandles. Finally, we study the corresponding action of the virtual braid group. For this action, the orbit multiplicities alone give a complete classification for every quandle of order at most four.

papers.title: Sensor Monitoring Towards Industry 4.0: Bridging Concepts on the $C_n$ Multivariate Control Chart
papers.abstract: The main challenge in monitoring multiple sensors is the high dimensionality that a process can easily reach. From a decision-making perspective, converting these multivariate dynamics into an informative visualization is also not trivial. Statistical Process Control (SPC) techniques detect changes in quality characteristics, but they are difficult to apply beyond the normality (Gaussian) assumption. For instance, the most well-known SPC multivariate control chart is based on Hotelling's $T^2$ statistic, which assumes that the process data follow a multivariate normal distribution (which rarely occurs in practice) and that the observations are serially independent. This study focuses on the multivariate case (dimension $d \geq 2$), regardless of the data dependence or marginal asymmetry. We propose a new control chart for change detection in copula-based multivariate processes, called the $C_n$-chart, which is based on a density level-set tolerance region built from a copula function, and we derive its run-length properties. The methodology also quantifies the (not necessarily linear) dependence among the variables. Two case studies are presented, one on water quality control and the other on monitoring brass-steel thermostats, complemented by a simulation study of run-length performance and computational cost. The results show that the proposed methodology captures both the association among variables and the anomalies, and that it accommodates variable selection through conditional (regression) modeling of the margins.

papers.title: Chromatic heights of homotopy fixed points of iterated topological Hochschild homology of connective spectra
papers.abstract: Let $R$ be an $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$-ring spectrum of height $m$. The chromatic redshift theorem implies that its $n$-fold iterated algebraic $K$-theory $K^{(n)}(R)$ has height $m+n$. Moreover, there is a natural map $K^{(n)}(R)\to (T^n\otimes R)^{hT^n}$, where $T^n\otimes R$ denotes the $n$-fold iterated topological Hochschild homology. Hence it is natural to ask whether the target also has height $m+n$. Although this fails in general, we prove that it holds whenever $R$ is connective and $m\geq1$. Our proof is based on an iterative calculation using Wilson spaces and relative topological Hochschild homology. As an application, we determine the support of the $T^n$-homotopy fixed points of $n$-fold iterated topological Hochschild homology of $\mathrm{BP}\langle m\rangle$ for $n=2,3$ with $\mathrm{BP}\langle m\rangle$ equipped with any $\mathbb{E}_3$-$\mathrm{MU}$-form.

papers.title: NEXONN: Advancing the NEXOTRANS Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval Framework with Transformer-Based Neural Posterior Estimation for JWST Transmission Spectroscopy of WASP-39b
papers.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope is delivering unprecedented constraints on exoplanet atmospheres, but computationally intensive Bayesian retrievals challenge the transition from individual planets to population-level studies of planetary formation and evolution. We introduce NEXONN, a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow framework within NEXOTRANS that enables rapid atmospheric posterior estimation with uncertainty quantification. Incorporating PandExo-based JWST noise, we benchmark NEXONN against PyMultiNest using simulated spectra and JWST observations of WASP-39 b (0.6-12 microns). For simulated MIRI/LRS data, eight posteriors achieve a mean overlap of 80.32%. Retrievals of combined NIRISS, NIRSpec, and MIRI observations yield consistent atmospheric properties. For the full dataset, NEXONN infers C/O = 0.82 (+0.01/-0.02) and [M/H] = 1.13 (+0.04/-0.04), compared with PyMultiNest values of 0.80 (+0.03/-0.01) and 1.19 (+0.05/-0.03). Divergence metrics, Wasserstein distances, posterior overlaps, and coverage tests assess posterior fidelity and uncertainty calibration, revealing parameter-dependent differences. Once trained, NEXONN performs posterior inference within seconds, enabling scalable population studies of exoplanet atmospheric composition, formation, and evolution.

papers.title: Metrics-in-the-Loop: Complexity Feedback Reshapes Agent-Written Code
papers.abstract: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.

papers.title: RoboDx: Repair and Diagnosis of Faults in Robot Software
papers.abstract: A patch to a robot's navigation software can pass every unit test and still drive the robot off its path. Checking how the repaired robot drives catches such patches. It does not show that the agent found everything that was wrong. We introduce RoboDx, a generator of repair tasks for simulated robot navigation software with known injected faults. A hidden verifier marks a repair as verified only if the robot then drives correctly in hidden scenarios, which the agent never sees. A second track hides the code and asks the agent to pick the cause from a list of hypotheses. A task with two faults can contain a quiet fault, a fault that makes no hidden scenario fail unless the other fault is also present. On our set of 100 tasks, RoboDx-Hard-100, almost every repair by Claude Opus 5.5 with standard coding tools is verified. We analyse 94 of the tasks, 44 with one fault and 50 with two. On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of Opus's 49 verified repairs remove both injected edits. Most faults left behind are configuration constants whose correct value the task's documentation does not state. Opus names both faults on 10/50 of these tasks when it cannot see the code. We then give four current models the same measurements of each faulty robot, picked so that, in the simulator, only the true cause produces all of them. The models name the cause on at most 38 of 94 tasks. They are right on almost all when they also get the simulator's output for every hypothesis. Their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain. On 97 tasks from real bug-fix pull requests, Claude Haiku 5.5, the weakest model on the generated tasks, scores lowest, and the other three models are not ordered.

papers.title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.

papers.title: SWIFT: Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely Action for Asynchronous Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Driving scenes keep changing during model computation, making both observation freshness and action-delivery time central to world-action planning. To retain rich generative world priors in autonomous driving without stalling real-time control, we present SWIFT (Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely action), a deployment-oriented asynchronous world-action system that moves world updates off the observation-to-action critical path. On a background GPU, a slow Video DiT streams surround-view history into read-only predictive world context, trained with a predictive span that covers both the update interval and background world computation. On a foreground GPU, a lightweight freshness carrier encodes current surround-view images into a gated key/value bank at every step, letting a fast Action DiT combine live visual feedback with the latest completed world context without waiting. On open-loop NAVSIM, SWIFT reaches 94.2 PDMS at 198.4 ms per decision with a trajectory scorer; on closed-loop Bench2Drive, it achieves an 80.30 Driving Score at 109.9 ms foreground latency. SWIFT further transfers to the Waymo E2E hidden test (8.0050 Rater Feedback Score) and nuScenes (0.54 m mean endpoint error, 0.03% mean collision rate). Across all four benchmarks, SWIFT achieves the best results among compared world-action methods, establishing a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off.

papers.title: From Powers--Stormer to Loewner Inertia: Weighted Trace Functionals and Orthogonal Perturbations
papers.abstract: We study the weighted trace functional $\TT_{f,h}(A,B)=\Tr h^\circ(A-B)[f(A)-f(B)]$, where $h^\circ(H)=h(H_+)-h(H_-)$. The Jordan decomposition of $A-B$ yields exact common-roof decompositions for operator monotone and operator convex functions, including the Powers--Størmer and Ricard trace comparisons. The orthogonal cross term gives a finite rank-one realization of the classical conditional Löwner-matrix criterion for operator convexity. For powers, resolvent squares yield a coupling-dependent Mellin strip, endpoint identities, and quantitative bounds on off-sector spectral interactions. Linearization produces positive and inverse moment subspaces of power Löwner matrices. A confluent determinant calculation provides the remaining sign data in the known inertia classification. We give explicit equality conditions and a finite-copy application of the Powers--Størmer equality case.

papers.title: Fixed and periodic points of bi-dual intersection operators
papers.abstract: We classify the fixed and periodic points, up to positive dilation, of the operators $\mathbb I_m=\mathbb I_{m,m+1}$ in the indexed bi-dual intersection family associated with centro-section integrals. For $n\ge3$ and $1\le m\le n-2$, a star body satisfies $\mathbb I_m^{\,r}K=cK$ for some $c>0$ and an integer $r\ge1$ if and only if it is an origin-centered Euclidean ball. No convexity, origin symmetry, or initial differentiability is assumed. An exact Grassmannian graph representation gives a decreasing weight and yields a strictly positive linear increment under continuous Steiner symmetrization unless the body is already symmetric. At a fixed point, a uniform radial Taylor estimate makes the same volume-preserving increment quadratic. Sobolev estimates for the spherical Radon transform and its adjoint supply the required regularity. Independently, a strict Lyapunov inequality reduces every periodic point up to dilation to a fixed point. We also prove automatic positivity and smoothness for bounded nonnegative solutions and local geometric convergence of normalized iterates near the ball.

papers.title: Stephen: Verifying Sequencer-Aided Coordination Systems with Cross-View Prophecy
papers.abstract: Many distributed systems achieve high performance by relying on dedicated sequencers to order requests, leaving replicas to commit them in that order. Despite more than a decade of such sequencer-aided coordination (SAC) systems, from Corfu and NOPaxos to LazyLog and SwitchBFT, their correctness has been argued only with pen-and-paper proofs or bounded model checking at the protocol level. In this paper, we formally verify implementations of SAC protocols. The sequencer seems to make this easy: it decides the order of all requests, so the proof can place each request's linearization point at the sequencer using a well-known technique, prophecy variables. Yet a linearization point placed at the sequencer is not durable, because the sequencer orders a request before any replica commits it. Crashes and other rare events may trigger a view change that discards the request, nullifying the earlier decision and the proof that rests on it. Our framework, Stephen, extends prophecy variables to handle view changes, and we make three contributions. (1) We develop cross-view prophecy peek, which lets the proof follow a request across view changes until it is either committed or permanently discarded. (2) Our verification uncovered bugs in existing SAC implementations, including one that can lose committed requests. We fix them and prove the fixes correct. (3) We apply Stephen to NOPaxos, Corfu and LazyLog. We build verified implementations with machine-checked proofs of linearizability. They perform within 17% of their open-source, unverified counterparts. The verified implementations and proofs will be open-sourced.

papers.title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

papers.title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory of Process Memory and Measurement Records
papers.abstract: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.

papers.title: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards
papers.abstract: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

papers.title: Sightline: Long-Window Speculative Decoding for Fast SVG Generation
papers.abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation models write a graphic as code with one forward pass per token, so drawing is slow. Speculative decoding speeds them up losslessly, and block drafters guess many tokens per pass. On SVG, many of their rounds accept the whole draft and end only at the verification window. We find that their misses are rare and clumped, and that they stay accurate far deeper into a block than on natural language. A run-length identity and three propositions show that a longer window pays once the candidates are wide, up to the drafter's horizon. We propose Sightline, which pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Experiments cover text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from MMSVG, MMSVG-2M and SArena. In every setting, Sightline is the fastest of the compared lossless decoders. On SArena, it stays the fastest when every decoder shares one loop control. It also leads in almost every setting of six models from four other families, which write SVG code, compressed SVG tokens or Lottie JSON. Analyses trace the lead to rounds that shorter windows cut off, both in loop-free content and in loops. Speculative decoding also saves time for choosing samples by rendering, which beats choosing by likelihood. These results suggest that speculative decoding on vector graphics should verify as far as the drafter sees. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/Sightline.

papers.title: Breaking the Myth of Four-Tier Stacked Transistors for Logic: an Investigation from Process to Device and Block-Level PPA
papers.abstract: For the first time, this work evaluated whether 4-tier stacked transistors can translate the straightforward density gains into realistic chip-level scaling benefits. A practical dual-sided 4-tier transistor-stacking CFFET (Flipped CFET-to-CFET) process was proposed, on which a DTCO framework spanning standard-cell design, local interconnects, RO analysis, and physical implementation was built under 2A node design rules. The CFFET was also benchmarked with its 2-tier transistor-stacking counterparts FFET. Among CFFET configurations, the best-performing Symmetric Power still lags FFET by 11.2% in RO frequency due to the complex MOL parasitics. At the block level, CFFET reduces the Ibex RISC-V core area by only 12.8% (far below the 40% nominal cell-height reduction), while running 10.9% slower at iso-power. We further introduced a novel Tetris-like cell stitching to minimize the area overhead, which allows non-rectangular cell design and recovers 7.4% area in a 1-bit ALU design. An optimized NanoStack CFFET was finally proposed, inspired by previous work. This work indicates that straightforward vertical 4-tier stacking proves insufficient to guarantee enough PPA benefits, though the resulting design insights may guide future advanced architectures.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic limit of the Toda lattice
papers.abstract: In this paper we consider the Toda lattice under random, spatially inhomogeneous initial data, meaning that its initial momenta and interparticle spacings are independent and their laws may slowly vary in space. When the density is strictly positive (but sufficiently small), we identify the model's hydrodynamic limit under Euler scaling. More precisely, we prove that spatial averages of each of the model's local conserved quantities converge to moments of a density $m_τ(λ,q)$ solving the generalized hydrodynamic equation predicted by Doyon arXiv:1902.07624 and Spohn arXiv:1902.07751. To do so, we justify the notion that the Toda lattice can be thought of as a dense collection of many "quasiparticles" that interact through scattering. As in Aggarwal arXiv:2503.08018, we define these quasiparticles through spectral properties of the Toda Lax matrix, but in our inhomogeneous setting we must now show that the eigenvectors of this Lax matrix remain localized throughout the dynamics. The core of our work is to show that, with high probability, the quasiparticle trajectories converge to the characteristic curves of the generalized hydrodynamic equation.

papers.title: TacPilot: Does Touch Need to Be Everywhere?
papers.abstract: Tactile feedback helps visual manipulation policies respond to local contact, but changes in tactile observations do not always require corrective motion, and sustained corrections do not always require new tactile features. We introduce TacPilot, a tactile residual framework that separates representation updates from action intervention around a frozen visual policy. TacPilot uses a perception gate to determine when tactile features need refreshing and updates only affected regions while reusing unchanged features. A separate intervention gate determines whether bounded Cartesian and gripper residuals modify the nominal visual action. This separation allows tactile perception and action correction to follow different spatial and temporal demands during manipulation. In offline expert-trajectory replay, local feature reuse reduces encoded regions by 56.4% relative to periodic full encoding, with essentially unchanged action predictions. In an exploratory simulation evaluation spanning two cylinder sizes, TacPilot succeeds in 26 of 30 trials (86.7%). We further validate TacPilot on OpenArm v2 equipped with Paxini tactile sensors across four contact-rich manipulation tasks.

papers.title: CoT-WAM: Collaborative Training of Vision-Language Models and World-Action Models via Plan Latents
papers.abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.

papers.title: SFiD: Self-Supervised Fitness-Driven Optimization for Next-Generation Networking
papers.abstract: Next-generation (NG) wireless networks face increasingly complex and dynamic optimization challenges driven by data-intensive applications and massive device connectivity. Existing methods suffer from one or more limitations, including high computational complexity, poor scalability and adaptability, reliance on large labeled datasets, or weak generalization in dynamic and non-convex wireless environments. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a self-supervised fitness-driven diffusion (SFiD) method that autonomously generates its own training data and iteratively learns from it. It also exhibits strong generalization capabilities and the ability to effectively tackle challenging optimization problems. We validate the convergence of our proposed method to the global optimum on both analytical convex and non-convex optimization problems. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we consider reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) phaseshift optimization in cell-free massive multiple-input multipleoutput (CF-mMIMO) systems with imperfect channel state information and spatial correlation at the RIS as a case study. Specifically, we develop SFiD-C for continuous variable optimization and apply it to optimize continuous RIS phase shifts in CF-mMIMO systems. We also develop SFiD-D for discrete variable optimization and apply it to optimize discrete RIS phase shifts in CF-mMIMO systems. Furthermore, we develop a binary neural network (BNN) based version of SFiDD for reducing its computational complexity, referred to as SFiD-D (BNN). Finally, our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods markedly improve computational efficiency and achieve comparable or superior performance compared to meta-heuristic and DRL benchmarks for both continuous and discrete RIS phase-shift optimization.

papers.title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
papers.abstract: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.

papers.title: On pluriclosed torsion-critical Hermitian metrics
papers.abstract: In our previous work, we studied the squared $L^2$-norm functionals $\mathcal G$ of Gauduchon's torsion $1$-form and $\mathcal F$ of the Chern torsion over the space of all Hermitian metrics with unit volume on a compact complex manifold. We introduced torsion-critical metrics as critical points of $\mathcal F$. In this paper, We prove that a pluriclosed and astheno-Kähler metric is torsion-critical if and only if it is Kähler. In particular, every compact pluriclosed torsion-critical Hermitian threefold is Kähler. We also give explicit examples and derive geometric consequences under additional curvature assumptions.

papers.title: Character codegrees in $π$-separable groups
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the set $\operatorname{C}_π(G)$ of irreducible characters of a finite $π$-separable group $G$ whose codegrees (defined by Qian as $\operatorname{cod}(χ)=|G:\kerχ|/χ(1)$) are $π$-numbers, in relation to the Isaacs--Gajendragadkar classes of $π$-special characters $\operatorname{X}_π(G)$ and $\operatorname{B}_π$-characters $\operatorname{B}_π(G)$.

papers.title: Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
papers.abstract: This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting. The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used. Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted. The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2). Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) separates long-run trends from monsoon and crop-cycle seasonality. A non-negative PCA gives sign-consistent, interpretable weights and rankings nearly identical to standard PCA ($ρ$ = 0.998). Across districts, the index explains 74% of the variation in the NFHS-5 wealth index, 52% in household consumption (HCES 2023-24) and about 78% in real district GDP levels (65% in logs), but does not track short-run output growth. Because it measures structural capacity rather than annual output, the index kept rising through the FY2020-21 COVID-19 contraction. Across Maharashtra's six revenue divisions, relative inequality fell by 44% even as the absolute gap between leading and lagging divisions widened by 32%; district-level $β$-convergence implies a half-life of about 14 years. The framework offers a scalable, deflator-free basis for structural monitoring in data-sparse economies.

papers.title: Sharp orthonormal Strichartz estimates for the Schrödinger equation in all remaining cases
papers.abstract: We study orthonormal Strichartz estimates for the free Schrödinger equation in homogeneous Sobolev spaces $\dot H^s$. We resolve the remaining open cases concerning the optimal summability of the coefficients. Together with earlier results and counterexamples, our theorems complete the classification for nonnegative Sobolev regularity $0\le s<d/2$.

papers.title: Critical--localized reentry under periodic spacer control
papers.abstract: Tracking a fixed fraction of a quasiperiodic spectrum tests whether repeated critical--localized alternation extends over a nonzero spectral weight. We find such alternation in a matched-dimer chain by varying only the spacer on-site energies and following a fixed interval of integrated-density-of-states (IDS) labels. An exact Bloch-determinant identity links the physical transfer discriminant to the bands of a periodic reference operator. For the golden cell frequency, we prove that, on a common full-measure set of phases and for every finite value of the spacer control, the physical spectrum in the open reference bands is critical, with purely singular-continuous spectrum and zero Lyapunov exponent, while the spectrum strictly outside the bands is pure point, with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions. Validated IDS bounds certify repeated critical--localized alternation of the same fixed spectral fraction at successive spacer controls. Spacer shifts move the physical levels and reference-band edges at different rates, allowing us to reshape finite-chain return windows and place their endpoints at prescribed controls. An affine recalibration relocates the control family exactly.

papers.title: A Dual-SOM Learner Model of Instructional Efficiency within Cognitive Load Theory
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel methodological framework, integrating a dual self-organising map (SOM) neural network architecture with Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), for assessing instructional efficiency within learning environments. By representing curriculum content as a directed acyclic graph of topic dependencies, the proposed model captures collective learning behaviour across two core dimensions: academic performance and subjective/introspective mental effort. During SOM training, representative data sets of successful learner trajectories are compressed into two topologically ordered, identically structured neural networks: PSOM (performance space) and ESOM (mental effort space). By pairing these behavioural maps, the model serves as a decision-support tool that enables instructors to simultaneously pinpoint structural instructional design defects, such as hidden topic prerequisites, and evaluate collective cognitive load profiles.
