One sentence appended to the system prompt cut Sonnet's cheats on the same 60 tasks from 22 to 8 (an AI reviewer will read the transcript), 6 (a person will review the work), 6 ("This session is recorded.") and 1 (do not special-case tests), all significant under exact McNemar tests, with honest passes unchanged. No remaining cheat moved to a shell falsely described as unrecorded (0 of 4). Asked for a final report, every one of 55 natural cheats named its special case; unasked, Sonnet and Opus said nothing in 52 of 52. An LLM judge caught all 55; deterministic rules over the host record caught 27. A scripted tamper demonstration, with keyword stand-ins for the judges, shows that one rewrite of the agent-side transcript hides two calls from a judge that reads it, while the signed record keeps them; in a 40-rollout pilot, Sonnet never touched its transcript. The judge and the record caught different things, which leads to our main conclusion: the record is the evidence a judge should read, not a replacement for one. All pre-registrations, results documents, code and evidence manifests are released.

papers.title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
papers.abstract: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.

papers.title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain.

papers.title: A Perspective on Topological Charge Density Wave Materials
papers.abstract: Charge density waves are among the earliest known ordered states in quantum materials, yet they have re-emerged at the center of modern discussions of topology, symmetry breaking, and collective dynamics. In several material classes, charge-density-wave order reshapes electronic bands, boundary states, defect structures, and electromagnetic responses in ways that invite a topological interpretation. Real-space imaging has shown that incommensurate order can form networks of phase defects rather than uniform modulations. Boundary-resolved spectroscopy has revealed in-gap modes whose existence and spatial structure track the charge-density-wave order, although such observations remain confined to a single material family. In Weyl materials, density-wave gaps have been linked to axion-like magnetoelectric response, placing the charge-density-wave phase within a dynamical-field description of the effective action. In kagome metals, charge order is intertwined with Berry curvature, unconventional symmetry breaking, and superconductivity. These developments have led to the term "topological charge density wave," but the phrase describes several physically distinct phenomena. We distinguish three meanings: (i) topology of the order parameter and its defects, (ii) topology of the charge-density-wave-reconstructed electronic structure and its boundary modes, and (iii) axion-like electromagnetic response generated by density-wave order. The experimental and theoretical support for these three meanings differs substantially. This Perspective traces the development of these ideas, clarifies the evidence behind each class, identifies unresolved questions and points of debate, and outlines experimental criteria for establishing topology in charge-density-wave states.

papers.title: Measuring and Attributing Evidence Sensitivity in Medical Vision-Language Models via Symmetric Counterfactual Controls
papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) asked closed clinical questions ("Is there a polyp?") can score well by relying on the question rather than the image, and current hallucination benchmarks cannot separate true visual discrimination from editing shortcuts or shifts in the answer threshold. We introduce a Counterfactual Evidence Framework that pairs each lesion erasure with a shape- and tool-matched control edit elsewhere in the image, adds same-site ring controls, restored and partial erasures, degraded views and natural negatives, tests on held-out inpainting tools, separates discrimination (the Evidence Sensitivity Gap, ESG, and AUROC) from the answer threshold, and checks the labels with blinded physician readers and hidden-state probes. Across 507 main-test cases (1,115 views), nine frontier VLMs claim 41.1% to 61.6% of erased lesions (ESG 0.269 to 0.470), whereas MedScope-4B, a Qwen3.5-4B agent trained on automatically built counterfactual trajectories, claims 9.6% (ESG 0.758; p <= 0.001 in all 27 primary comparisons). Physician readers support automated erasure in colonoscopy, where frontier models still claim 45% of erased lesions against 1% for MedScope-4B, but call a finding present on 54.7% of pooled erased reads across all sources, which bounds what unverified erasure can certify. Across 12 pre-registered training or system arms and 270 decision policies screened under a rule fixed in advance, every apparent utility gain comes from shifting the threshold rather than improving held-out discrimination, and probes point to perception as the remaining limit. We also report a 0/48 pneumothorax failure on an external cohort; retraining with pneumothorax patients in every stage finds 53% of pneumothoraxes on new patients without changing the main-test results.

papers.title: One Measurement, Many Fronts in Kitaev and Cluster Chains
papers.abstract: A projective measurement of one site in the ground state of a quantum chain disturbs the chain in two ways: learning the outcome shifts distant expectation values at once, through ground-state correlations, and the measurement erases the correlations between the measured site and the rest. Both changes travel outward. We solve this problem exactly for the Kitaev chain, the cluster chain in a transverse field, and the Kitaev chain with power-law couplings, and we find that far from the measured site every quadratic observable responds through a front. Where the front is and how fast it broadens depend only on the quasiparticle dispersion. How strong it is depends on two operators: how strongly the measured one creates the fastest quasiparticles and how strongly the observed one detects them; if either factor vanishes, the front is weaker and decays faster. One measurement therefore launches many fronts, one per observable, with a common position and width but different decay laws. In the Kitaev chain the density and the bond energy, the two terms of its nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian, respond to one density measurement with decay laws that trade places between the topological and the trivial phase; in the cluster chain, measuring a symmetry-odd spin instead of a symmetry-even one changes the critical decay law at a fixed Hamiltonian; and with power-law couplings the width law itself changes. All decay laws and profiles are obtained in closed form.

papers.title: A Physically Informed Changepoint Score for Fault Prioritisation in District Heating
papers.abstract: Poorly cooling district-heating installations raise return temperatures and pumped flow, increasing heat losses and pumping energy and hindering low-temperature operation. Faults often go unreported for weeks, so their onset is unknown and energy is wasted in the meantime. Utilities flag poorly cooling installations by a low supply-return temperature difference, but not when the problem began. Changepoint detectors such as the Bayesian Estimator of Abrupt Change, Seasonality, and Trend (BEAST) can date a change but report only its probability, so a large, fault-like change and a marginal one can look alike. We therefore develop a decision score that weighs each BEAST change in temperature difference and flow by its probability, size, deviation from recent operation and physical direction. Joint falls in temperature difference and rises in flow, the signature of insufficient cooling, rank first. Across 1,522 cases, 648 with a reported fault, 24 of the 25 highest-ranked cases were reported faults, and Average Precision was 0.772 against a prevalence of 0.426, likely conservative, as unreported cases may contain faults. Without using the report date, the strongest flow rise in reported-fault cases came a median of 11 days before the report (128 days in comparison cases). Combined with temperature-difference screening, the score raised Average Precision in season-matched cases from 0.486 to 0.646. After the detected change, flagged reported-fault installations returned water 16 K warmer and about half their circulated water delivered no heat. The score gives utilities a short list for inspection and a candidate onset date for each change.

papers.title: The Hibi--Li (2016) conjecture is fully resolved
papers.abstract: Hibi and Li conjectured that the order polytope $\mathcal{O}(P)$ of a finite poset $P$ has at most as many faces of each dimension as its chain polytope $\mathcal{C}(P)$, and that equality in some dimension $k$ with $1\leq k\leq|P|-1$ forces the two polytopes to be unimodularly equivalent. Fourier proved the inequality in a 2026 preprint. Let $X$ be the five-element poset in which an element lies above two incomparable elements and below two other incomparable elements. Using two results from Fourier's preprint, we show that if an $n$-element poset contains $X$ as an induced subposet, then, for every $k$ with $2\leq k\leq n-1$, its chain polytope has at least $\binom{n-3}{k-2}$ more $k$-dimensional faces than its order polytope, and that for every $n\geq5$ some $n$-element poset containing $X$ attains all these bounds at once. Since Hibi and Li showed that $\mathcal{O}(P)$ and $\mathcal{C}(P)$ are unimodularly equivalent exactly when $P$ does not contain $X$, this proves the equality statement for these values of $k$. The second version of Fourier's preprint gives an independent proof of this statement. For $k=1$, the equality statement is false: the polytopes $\mathcal{O}(X)$ and $\mathcal{C}(X)$ have the same number of edges (Hibi, Li, Sahara and Shikama) but are not unimodularly equivalent. Together with Fourier's inequality, these results settle the conjecture.

papers.title: The Digital-Energy Recomposition of the Kitchin Cycle: Exploratory Evidence from U.S. IT and Irish Data-Centre Series (1995-2025)
papers.abstract: Using quarterly FRED and CSO Ireland data over 1995Q1-2025Q4, we examine whether U.S.\ IT investment and Irish data-centre electricity are recomposing the Kitchin cycle around energy- and compute-backed assets. Three findings stand out. First, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test locates a significant break in the U.S.\ IT-GDP correlation at 2014Q3 (sup-W $= 9.69$; $r$ falls from $+0.45$ to $-0.12$); the Fisher $r$-to-$z$ test survives Bonferroni adjustment ($z = +3.11$, $p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.006$), whereas the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI boundary does not ($p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.164$), so ``Strategic Decoupling'' pre-dates the AI Era by approximately six years. Second, in Ireland the synchronous AI-Era correlation between metered data-centre electricity and Real GDP is large ($r = +0.41$, $N = 16$) but \emph{collapses to $r \approx 0$ when Real GDP is replaced by Real GNP}, suggesting the headline is largely an artefact of the shared multinational tax-structure footprint between hyperscaler operations and Irish gross output. Third, the Irish cross-correlation profile is asymmetric in the opposite direction to a leading-indicator reading: the largest positive coefficients cluster on the $k < 0$ side (GDP precedes data-centre load), so compute capacity is better read as coincident or moderately lagging. Given the small AI-Era samples and the absence of a quarterly multinational-adjusted aggregate such as GNI*, all coefficients are exploratory; subject to these caveats, the U.S.\ Kitchin cycle is best dated to 2014Q3, and the Irish Energy-Data Nexus is dominated by multinational firm activity.

papers.title: Evidence for Kaluza-Klein excitations of the graviton, gluon and quark at LHC
papers.abstract: Following our paper showing evidence for a tower of Kaluza-Klein gravitons, we interpret the massive 4 jet excesses observed by CMS. They could come from the decay of two heavy KK gluons gkk(3.6TeV) and gkk(8.6TeV) into pairs of KK quarks qkk(1TeV) and qkk(2.1TeV). Present limits on gkk into top pairs seem to exclude gkk(3.6TeV) but these limits assume a dominant decay into top pairs, which can be questioned as was the case in our study of KK graviton decays. The cross section predicted for gkk(8.6) requires a BR into a pair of qkk(2.1TeV) or order 10% which is not unlikely. We also discuss the issue of a hierarchy between the KK graviton masses and the vector boson masses and the solution provided by the RS multi-brane models. Prospects for reaching a 6 s.d. level local evidence with RUN3 data are promising for 3 channels. KK excitations of the Z boson are discussed and appear also promising. Indirect evidences for these particles are also presented.

papers.title: Geometric state space, memory representation and architectures
papers.abstract: We introduce a geometric framework for deriving attention architectures. A sequence forms a memory $m\in M_n$, and an attention pairing $ρ_n\colon M_n\to\operatorname{Hom}(A,A)$ determines how that memory acts on each token state. Different representations of this action recover familiar architectures: softmax attention reads individual key--value pairs, linear attention accumulates their contributions in matrix statistics, and Intention fits a regression map from keys to values. The framework also suggests new architectures by changing the geometry of the query--key pairing, the function carried by each value, or the space representing the memory. ImageNet-1K experiments illustrate these constructions through geometric CAFormer variants, a ViT with query-dependent values, and a linear ViT with a wider memory representation.

papers.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

papers.title: Stochastic gravitational waves from narrow-band cosmological magnetic fields
papers.abstract: We calculate the spectrum of gravitational waves generated by a cosmological magnetic field with a narrow-band power spectrum. For a magnetic spectrum narrowly peaked at a comoving wavenumber $k_c$, we find that the gravitational wave signal has a maximum at $2k_c$ and, as expected from momentum conservation, has a sharp cutoff at that scale. We apply this analysis to an ultralight dark matter model of magnetogenesis operating around recombination, in which an axion-photon coupling generates a helical magnetic field by parametric resonance. We determine the conditions for the resulting gravitational waves to enter the frequency range of pulsar timing experiments. Although the required frequency can be reached for sufficiently large coupling, the corresponding amplitude is below the experimental sensitivity for physically allowed energy densities of the magnetic field. We generalize this conclusion to models of magnetogenesis operating at other epochs, estimating as $T \simeq 160$ MeV the temperature of a magnetogenesis process assumed to be the source of the stochastic gravitational wave background suggested by pulsar timing arrays. We place the lower bound $T \gtrsim 1$-10 MeV on such viable models.

papers.title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy response prediction using pretreatment diffusion and contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging with clinical variables
papers.abstract: Prediction of pathological complete response before neoadjuvant chemotherapy may facilitate more tailored therapeutic planning for breast cancer patients. This work proposes a deep-learning model for pretreatment data only, combining apparent diffusion coefficient maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and clinical variables. The study uses the public ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2 multicenter dataset. The architecture employs EfficientNet-B0 pretrained encoders for image feature extraction and late fusion with clinical information. Multiple clinical variables were evaluated, including age, race, histological type, HR/HER2 subtype, SBR grade, and maximum diameter. Only HR/HER2 subtype improved the average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and was retained in the final model. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation, standalone apparent diffusion coefficient maps achieved a mean AUC of 0.79, whereas dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging achieved 0.74. Adding HR/HER2 subtype improved performance to 0.83 and 0.81, respectively. The final configuration, using both imaging modalities and HR/HER2 subtype, achieved an AUC of 0.86. These results support pretreatment multimodal learning for response prediction, although external validation is required before clinical use.

papers.title: Thermoelectric properties of metal-semiconductor percolation composites
papers.abstract: We analyze the thermoelectric response of composite materials comprising homogeneous semiconductor hosts with randomly distributed metallic inclusions. We demonstrate that the properties of such materials are strongly affected by the percolation transition (with background conductivity). We show that in the vicinity of the percolation threshold, the power factor and the thermoelectric figure of merit strongly depend on both the concentration and arrangement of inclusions. Finally, we identify promising regimes for enhancing the power factor in realistic composites.

papers.title: XPCS-Echo and broad relaxation measurements using a bunch-mode data acquisition scheme
papers.abstract: Echoes observed in the intensity-intensity autocorrelation functions [$g_2(q, τ)$] is a powerful method for probing nonaffine deformations and yielding behavior of soft viscoelastic materials subjected to an oscillatory shear. Multispeckle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) measurements of large number of echoes with high time resolution impose severe constraints in terms of the computational hardware and potential degradation of the sample. These issues are alleviated by implementing a bunch-mode data acquisition scheme in which the highest resolution frames or bunches centered at the echo peaks. In addition, by placing the bunches in an aperiodic Fibonacci sequence, $g_2(q, τ)$ over a long time span can be measured with orders of magnitude lesser number of frames. The performance of these XPCS acquisition schemes is demonstrated using slowly relaxing model colloidal suspensions. Furthermore, an analytical expression is provided for the quantitative description of full $g_2(q, τ)$.

papers.title: VOS: Variate Ordering Strategies for Skyline Query Optimization
papers.abstract: Efficiency of skyline algorithms is highly influenced by the underlying data characteristics. Traditionally, optimization efforts have focused on minimizing the total number of tuple-pair dominance checks to improve query performance. However, in practice, a dominance check between two tuples does not necessarily require evaluating dominance relationships for each and every preference attribute of the data and this creates a disconnect between dominance checks optimization and query execution performance. In this paper, we argue that skyline algorithms need to optimize total per-attribute dominance checks, along with per-tuple dominance checks and that, for both of these goals, the ordering of the attributes (or variates) can have a substantial impact on the efficiency of skyline computation. Based on this premise, we present several strategies for identifying an effective variate order to minimize redundant attribute comparisons. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and on both scalar and SIMD architectures, confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach in reducing computational overhead and improving skyline query performance.

papers.title: The Best of Times, the Worst of Times: Moment-Based Analysis of Probabilistic Cost Structures
papers.abstract: Many practical costs---such as the completion time of a quantum repeater, the rounds of an RFID collision-resolution protocol, or the response time of a fork--join computation---are described by hierarchical cost expressions: a tree of independent subcomputations with nonnegative integer costs, combined by addition, max, and min. We compute their moments with sound error bounds. Moment-based analyses for additive costs do not apply, because the moments of $\max(X,Y)$ are not determined by those of $X$ and $Y$; propagating full distributions becomes expensive as trees grow; and scalable approximations are hand-derived for specific structures and lack error bounds. Our analysis proceeds bottom-up, summarizing each subtree by a surrogate distribution: an exact short-horizon prefix plus a compact parametric tail fitted to preserve the queried moment. Each prefix is computed exactly from the children's prefixes---for a retry, whose cost sums an unbounded number of attempts, by solving a local recurrence equation---so all approximation is confined to the tails. Abstraction introduces shape error but no moment error; nonlinear operators, such as max and min, convert shape error into moment error. The analysis tracks two bounds, one on shape error and one on moment error. Tracking both lets it report a sound interval for the mean, the second moment, and the variance. Lengthening the prefix, or solving subtrees exactly, narrows the interval at the cost of additional computation. For quantum-repeater chains of up to 4096 links with high swap-success probability, our Dickens tool bounds the mean completion time within 1%, whereas the exact Markov-chain solution exhausts memory with 16 links, and the best hand-derived approximation we evaluated has 47% error with 64 links. Dickens also bounds second moments, variances, and deadline-miss probabilities, and handles RFID and fork--join costs.

papers.title: Bringing Back Rule Induction to Fluid Intelligence Research? An Initial Validation of the ARC-AGI Benchmark in Humans
papers.abstract: Two competing perspectives on fluid intelligence (gf) measures propose that performance is primarily constrained either by working memory capacity or by the ability to induce novel relations. The first perspective is currently dominant in measurement, as evident from the use of a limited set of recurring rules, whereas the second perspective is reflected in many definitions but rarely present in measurement. The ARC-AGI benchmark predominantly requires rule induction and was proposed as a measure of gf for both humans and artificial systems. However, its psychometric properties have not yet been examined in human samples. We therefore investigated the psychometric characteristics and nomological network of ARC-AGI in a first study with 100 participants. A compilation of ARC-AGI items showed good psychometric properties and correlated substantially with figural fluid intelligence as measured by a figural reasoning test ($ρ$ = .63). Associations with figural originality were weak. These findings provide initial support for the validity of ARC-AGI as a measure of human fluid intelligence. Future research should include more rule induction tasks as well as additional multivariate covariates. This study is unusual by studying a task in humans that was initially designed for machines. We suggest systematically embedding AI benchmarks into the nomological network of human cognitive abilities to enable more systematic evaluation and interdisciplinary cooperation.

papers.title: Arbor: How Search Policy Shapes Agent Behavior in System Optimization
papers.abstract: Achieving peak performance on modern accelerators requires coordinated optimization across kernels, operator fusion, KV-cache management, quantization, scheduling, and communication overlap, a process that demands weeks of expert effort per model and hardware platform. We present Arbor, a system that gives autonomous agents an explicit optimization tree to reason over, backtrack through, and deepen with experience, with pluggable search policies, scored bandit traversal, parallel agent swarms, and depth-first sweep, sharing a common harness of containerized isolation, automatic rollback, and end-to-end validation. Arbor generalizes across domains: +40% to +193% on six production inference models across two GPU generations, +42.8% on LLM training, and +41% on recommendation training, where agents autonomously wrote kernel-level and framework-level optimizations spanning thousands of lines of code. In controlled ablations where every search policy receives the same agent, tree, and tools, we find that search structure shapes both the magnitude and the nature of the optimizations. The bandit achieves +30.1% through targeted framework fixes, the sweep +26.4% through deep kernel rewrites, and the swarm +33.4% by compounding independent changes. An agent-driven loop that receives the same harness, tools, and information, but selects its own targets reaches +14%, writing 4x more code per percentage point of improvement than Arbor's structured search policies. We additionally introduce an evaluation framework for autonomous loop-based agents spanning efficiency, grounding, robustness, and depth, designed to characterize agent search behavior across long-running optimization campaigns.

papers.title: Lepton $g-2$ non-universality of hadronic contributions and a sub-GeV window to New Physics
papers.abstract: We propose the linear combination of the anomalous magnetic moments of the muon and electron, $a_{μ-e} \equiv a_μ- (m_μ/m_e)^2 a_e$, as a natural low-energy window quantity that may directly probe the current discrepancy between the data-driven and lattice-QCD evaluations of hadronic contributions. The rescaling ensures an exact cancellation of the leading short-range ($m_\ell^2$-scaling) effects, thereby improving the UV behavior. Because entire classes of contributions cancel identically --- not merely in variance --- the combination is predictable in chiral perturbation theory with no free low-energy constant, and it isolates flavor-non-universal New Physics. The hadronic-vacuum-polarization effect in $a^{\rm HVP}_{μ-e}$, together with its uncertainty, is reduced as compared to $a^{\rm HVP}_μ$ by $\sim 85\%$. This is promising for tests of New Physics with some degree of flavor non-universality, conditional on significant improvements in the measurements of $a_e$ and $α$.

papers.title: Measuring What Matters: Synthetic Benchmarks for Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Concept bottleneck models predict using high-level concepts detected in inputs. Although these models provide a simple way to reap benefits from interpretability, they are hard to train and evaluate because very few real-world datasets include concept labels. In this paper, we develop synthetic benchmarks for concept bottleneck models. With our benchmarks, researchers can generate labeled datasets and control properties that affect performance, such as data modality, the choice of concepts, or annotation quality. They can thus find problems that suit these models and isolate the factors behind their failures. We demonstrate how our benchmarks can be used to evaluate major use cases for concept bottleneck models: decision support, i.e., helping human experts make better decisions; and automation, i.e., handling routine tasks without supervision. Our demonstrations show how the benchmarks can identify new failure modes and attribute them to either the architecture or the data.

papers.title: KVBuffer: IO-aware Serving for Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Linear attention has recently gained significant attention for long-context inference due to its constant decoding cost with respect to context length. However, existing serving systems typically serve linear attention by recurrently computing and updating a large linear attention state in every decoding step. Since the state is much larger than the per-token key and value, recurrent decoding incurs substantial memory access and becomes inefficient for serving linear attention. In this paper, we propose KVBuffer, an IO-aware serving mechanism for linear attention. By buffering recent keys and values, KVBuffer enables serving systems to compute linear attention outputs in more flexible and memory-efficient ways. For decoding, KVBuffer enables chunkwise computation, which reduces average memory access and decoding latency by deferring state updates and applying them in batch. For speculative decoding, KVBuffer verifies draft tokens in parallel and avoids storing temporary states. For short contexts, KVBuffer computes attention outputs directly from buffered keys and values, without creating or updating the linear attention state. We implement KVBuffer in SGLang for Qwen3.5 and Nemotron-3 series models. Our evaluations show that KVBuffer can speedup batch decoding by up to 1.47x and increase the maximum number of serving requests by 5x for speculative decoding when verifying four draft tokens.

papers.title: Inverse Design for Conditional Distribution Matching
papers.abstract: Generative models are powerful tools for sampling from a learned distribution $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X)$, and inverse-design methods invert this map to find an input $x$ that produces a desired point output $y^*$. However, many design goals are naturally distributional rather than pointwise, incorporating the inherent uncertainty of $Y$ and targeting a specific form for it, a task not addressed by standard inverse design. To address this issue we introduce Conditional Distribution Matching (CDM), a new inverse-design problem class in generative modeling: given a joint distribution $\mathcal{P}(X, Y)$ and a target distribution $\mathcal{G}(Y)$, find an input $x^*$ whose induced conditional distribution $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X = x^*)$ matches $\mathcal{G}$. We formally define two variants: Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling (CDMS) and Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization (CDMO). To solve these problems, we propose MLGD-F (Matching-Loss Guided Diffusion with a Fast inner sampler), a plug-and-play inference-time algorithm that combines a pretrained score-based diffusion model with a pretrained fast conditional sampler, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. By leveraging single-step conditional sampling, MLGD-F enables tractable gradient computation, making the estimation of $\mathcal{P}(Y \mid X)$ both memory-efficient and computationally lightweight. We validate MLGD-F on synthetic benchmarks, structured image transformations, and generative editing optimization, demonstrating reliable recovery of inputs whose conditional distributions match diverse user-specified targets, including discrete mixtures and continuous low-rank supports.

papers.title: Nuclear Spin Isomers and the Pauli Principle in Polaritonic Chemistry
papers.abstract: The Pauli principle has far-reaching consequences in quantum physics. Here, we investigate, for the first time, its implications, together with nuclear spin isomerism, in polaritonic chemistry. The theory is developed for a single and a few molecules as well as for an ensemble of molecules. As an explicit and detailed example we first present an accurate numerical description of a realistic situation involving two $^{14}$NH$_3$ molecules, existing as ortho and para spin isomers, in an infrared plasmonic cavity. Then, we generalize the approach for molecular ensembles using analytical considerations based on the Tavis-Cummings model and simulate the transmission spectrum of a Fabry-Pérot cavity filled with $^{14}$NH$_3$ gas using quantum mechanics. These results are directly relevant for recent gas-phase experiments studying rovibrational polaritons in molecules. Our findings undoubtedly demonstrate that the Pauli principle and nuclear spin isomerism significantly reshape collective light-matter coupling involving molecules with identical nuclei.

papers.title: Motif enrichment as a driver of scale-free behavior in rewired random regular graphs
papers.abstract: We study the statistics of rewired random regular graphs (RRGs) in a mixed ensemble, where the average number of triangles is controlled by the fugacity $λ$, while the number of vertices and the vertex degree are fixed. This model exhibits a phase transition at critical fugacity $λ_{cr}$ from a triangle-poor phase (TPP), in which the number of triangles is independent of the system size, to a triangle-rich phase (TRP), in which the number of triangles scales linearly with the system size. We estimate $λ_{cr}$ by comparing the entropy of TPP with the energy of TRP. Above $λ_{cr}$, the RRG becomes a two-phase system in which dense clusters are connected by a sparse scale-free sub-network characterized by a degree distribution, $P(d) \sim d^{-γ}$, with $γ\approx 2$, independent of the size of the whole graph and its degree. We attribute this behavior to an "emergent preferential attachment" induced by triangle motifs, describe the mechanism underlying its formation, and derive the exponent $γ$ within a mean-field approach. Numerically the clusters and the inter-cluster subnetwork are identified through the Ollivier-Ricci curvature of the edges: it is positive inside clusters and negative on the links that form the inter-cluster subnetwork. We find that most inter-cluster triangles are isosceles, with the base lying inside one cluster and the apex belonging to the inter-cluster network. It is conjectured that a spanning inter-cluster scale-free network is stabilized against complete defragmentation into a disconnected set of cliques, by a sparse, structurally rigid "gas" of such apex-shared isosceles triads.

papers.title: Statistical Validation of Computer Models: Global and Subdomain Hypothesis Testing
papers.abstract: Computer simulations play an important role in scientific discovery and engineering innovation. Reliable computer models enable virtual experimentation that reduces the need for costly and time-consuming physical testing. However, the credibility of such models hinges on rigorous statistical validation against real-world data. This paper develops a formal frequentist framework for both global and subdomain validation of computer models. We propose the Fourier Maximum Modulus Test (FMMT), which leverages kernel ridge regression (KRR) to estimate the discrepancy between the computer model and the physical process, followed by a frequency-domain test based on weighted generalized Fourier coefficients. The theoretical analysis establishes the asymptotic normality of these coefficients, also when calibration parameters are estimated, allowing for closed-form p-values. Simulation studies and a shear-layer experiment demonstrate that FMMT achieves high power, accurate Type I error control, and strong sensitivity to localized discrepancies.

papers.title: Unsupervised Skeleton-Based Action Segmentation via Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Vector Quantization
papers.abstract: We propose a novel hierarchical spatiotemporal vector quantization framework for unsupervised skeleton-based temporal action segmentation. We first introduce a hierarchical approach, which includes two consecutive levels of vector quantization. Specifically, the lower level associates skeletons with fine-grained subactions, while the higher level further aggregates subactions into action-level representations. Our hierarchical approach outperforms the non-hierarchical baseline, while primarily exploiting spatial cues by reconstructing input skeletons. Next, we extend our approach by leveraging both spatial and temporal information, yielding a hierarchical spatiotemporal vector quantization scheme. In particular, our hierarchical spatiotemporal approach performs multi-level clustering, while simultaneously recovering input skeletons and their corresponding timestamps. Lastly, extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks, including HuGaDB, LARa, and BABEL, demonstrate that our approach establishes a new state-of-the-art performance and reduces segment length bias in unsupervised skeleton-based temporal action segmentation.

papers.title: Reducing the Power Required for Multi-UAV Tethered Payload Transportation via a Rotating Equilibrium
papers.abstract: Collaborative aerial transportation of tethered payloads is fundamentally limited by space, power, and weight constraints. Conventional approaches rely on static equilibrium conditions, where each vehicle tilts to generate the forces that ensure they maintain a formation geometry that avoids aerodynamic interactions and collision. This horizontal thrust component represents a significant energy penalty compared to the ideal case in which each vehicle produces purely vertical thrust to lift the payload. Operating in tighter tether configurations can minimize this effect, but at the cost of either having to fly the vehicles in closer proximity, which risks collision, or significantly increasing the length of the tether, which increases complexity and reduces potential use-cases. We propose operating the tether-suspended flying system at a rotating equilibrium. By maintaining steady circular motion, centrifugal forces provide the necessary horizontal tether tension, allowing each quadrotor to generate purely vertical thrust and thus reducing the total force (and power) required compared to an equilibrium where the thrusts are not vertical. It also allows for a wider range of tether configurations to be used without sacrificing efficiency. Results demonstrate that rotating equilibria can reduce power consumption relative to static lifting by up to 20%, making collaborative aerial solutions more practically relevant.

papers.title: Model-independent ZH production cross section at FCC-ee
papers.abstract: This paper presents prospects for measuring the model-independent ZH production cross section at the FCC-ee using the recoil-mass method at center-of-mass energies of 240 GeV and 365 GeV. Analyses are carried out in the muon, electron, and hadronic decay modes of the associated Z boson. The event selections rely primarily on the kinematics of the reconstructed Z decay products, ensuring maximal independence from specific Higgs boson decay modes, while multivariate techniques are employed to further enhance sensitivity. The statistical interpretation of the leptonic and hadronic final states at 240 GeV, with an integrated luminosity of 10.8 ab$^{-1}$, yields relative precisions of 0.52% for the combined leptonic channels and 0.38% for the hadronic channel. Their full statistical combination leads to uncertainties of 0.31% at 240 GeV and 0.52% at 365 GeV, the latter assuming an integrated luminosity of 3.12 ab$^{-1}$. Dedicated statistical tests demonstrate model independence at the level of the obtained precision. This study presents the first consistent and combined analysis of the leptonic and hadronic final states for a model-independent ZH cross-section measurement at a future lepton collider, using a unified workflow and covering both $\sqrt{s} = 240$ and 365 GeV. It provides the most precise expected measurement of the ZH production cross section at future lepton colliders, with the degree of model independence demonstrated within the achieved precision.

papers.title: A shorter-width post-selected circuit for a truncated-Taylor Hamiltonian-evolution segment
papers.abstract: We present an ancilla-efficient, post-selected circuit construction for a truncated-Taylor approximation to short-time Hamiltonian evolution. The construction combines a binary Taylor-order register with mid-circuit measurement, reset, and reuse of the Hamiltonian-index register. Conditioned on the prescribed all-zero outcomes, the circuit implements the truncated Taylor approximation while maintaining coherence among the Taylor-order branches while permitting early termination after a failed post-selection. For Taylor cutoff $K$, a Hamiltonian containing $L$ terms, and an $n$-qubit system, the circuit uses $\left\lceil\log {(K+1)}\right\rceil +\left\lceil\log L\right\rceil+n $ qubits, and executes $\mathcal{O}(K)$ controlled Hamiltonian blocks in a complete segment. We analyze its post-selection probability and expected per-segment cost, and implement and evaluate the construction in Guppy[1,2]. The present work focuses on the low-width implementation of individual short-time propagation segments; coherent composition into a deterministic long-time simulation requires an additional amplification or compression mechanism and is left for future work.

papers.title: SoK: Market Microstructure for Decentralized Prediction Markets (DePMs)
papers.abstract: Decentralized prediction markets (DePMs) allow open participation in event-based wagering without fully relying on centralized intermediaries. We review the history of DePMs which date back to 2011 and includes hundreds of proposals. Perhaps surprising, modern DePMs like Polymarket deviate materially from earlier designs like Truthcoin and Augur v1. We use our review to present a modular workflow comprising eight stages: underlying infrastructure, market topic, share structure and pricing, market initialization, trading, market resolution, settlement, and archiving. For each module, we enumerate the design variants, analyzing trade-offs around decentralization, expressiveness, and manipulation resistance. We also identify open problems for researchers interested in this ecosystem.

papers.title: Separability and Submetrizability in Locally Convex Spaces
papers.abstract: We introduce the property of countable separation for a locally convex Hausdorff space $X$ and relate it to the existence of a metrizable coarser topology. Building on this, we demonstrate how the separability of $X$ is equivalent to the existence of a locally convex topology on the dual $X'$ that is metrizable and coarser than the weak topology $σ(X', X)$. This result generalizes known conditions for separability and provides a precise duality between separability and metrizability. We also show how to derive new and known conditions for the separability of $X$ from this characterization.

papers.title: How K-12 Teachers Adapt Generative AI to Local Classroom Demands: Cultural Distance Between GenAI Defaults and Everyday Teaching Practices
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is entering K-12 classrooms, but its default culture does not always fit local teaching. Existing accounts either treat this misfit as macro-level structural bias or examine it through single-case studies; neither captures how much work teachers must do to make outputs usable across tasks. This exploratory, theory-building qualitative study introduces cultural distance, the gap between GenAI's default cultural repertoire and the situated demands of teachers' practice. Through interviews with 30 K-12 teachers who frequently use GenAI, 10 each from South Africa, Taiwan, and the United States, we identified three levels defined by the effort teachers invested and whether it yielded a usable output: low (minor edits), mid (sustained prompting and revision), and high (structural gaps rooted in unsupported languages, undigitized knowledge, or policy filters that no teacher effort can close). We present cultural distance as a promising framework requiring further examination and draw implications for designers, policymakers, and educators.

papers.title: Tropical Lagrangian coamoebae and generalized dimer models
papers.abstract: We study the coamoebae of Lagrangian submanifolds of $(\mathbb{C}^\times)^n$, specifically how the combinatorics of their degenerations encodes the homological algebra of mirror coherent sheaves. Concretely, to a minimal free resolution $F^\bullet$ of a module $M$ over $\mathbb{C}[z_1^{\pm 1}, \dotsc, z_n^{\pm 1}]$ we associate a simplicial complex $T(F^\bullet) \subset T^n$. We call $T(F^\bullet)$ a tropical Lagrangian coamoeba. We show that the discrete information in $F^\bullet$ can often be recovered from $T(F^\bullet)$, and that more generally $M$ is mirror to a certain constructible sheaf supported on $T(F^\bullet)$. The resulting interplay between coherent sheaves on $(\mathbb{C}^\times)^n$ and simplicial complexes in $T^n$ provides a higher-dimensional generalization of the spectral theory of dimer models in $T^2$, as well as a symplectic counterpart to the theory of brane brick models.

papers.title: Collaborative Optimal Design of Controlled Experiments with Subject Covariates
papers.abstract: Modern experimental design problems often encounter multiple controlled experiments with subjects participating in more than one experiment. It is of interest to consider the optimal design of allocating subjects to treatment or control for these experiments especially when subject covariate information is available. In this work, we propose an optimal allocation method to enable accurate estimates of treatment effects for all experiments. Deriving the precision matrix of the treatment effects and using D-optimality as our allocation criterion, we demonstrate the advantage of collaboratively designing and analyzing multiple experiments over traditional independent design and analysis, and propose efficient algorithms to design construction of the D-optimality problem for collaborative experiments. The performance of the proposed methods is examined by simulation studies and a case study involving online education experimentation.

papers.title: Searching for cosmic strings via black hole spin-down
papers.abstract: Cosmic strings that are attached to rapidly spinning black holes can extract significant amounts of rotational energy and angular momentum. Here, we study the effect on primordial black holes, which are expected to form with one or more cosmic strings attached. Although large primordial black holes of mass greater than O$(10 M_\odot)$ are predicted to rapidly spin up due to accretion soon after forming, we argue that cosmic strings will spin them down again. We show that if there are cosmic strings with tension greater than $10^{-20}$, and, provided at least one remains attached, the spins of large primordial black holes should consequently be observed to be near zero. We also investigate the effect on a supermassive black hole of capturing a cosmic string and discuss the possibility of observing the subsequent spin down by its effect on a pulsar orbiting the black hole.

papers.title: Uniqueness of ground state solutions for fractional Schrödinger equations with general nonlinearities
papers.abstract: In 2013, R.L. Frank and E. Lenzmann [R.L. Frank, E. Lenzmann, Uniqueness of non-linear ground states for fractional Laplacians in $\mathbb{R}$, Acta Math. 210 (2) (2013) 261-318] studied the following problem: \begin{align*} (-Δ)^su + u = u^{p-1} \quad \text{in } \mathbb{R}^N, \end{align*} where $s \in (0,1)$, $N = 1$, $p \in (2,2_s^*)$, and $2_s^*$ is the critical fractional Sobolev exponent. They proved that the ground state is unique (up to translations). Then in 2016, they, together with L. Silvestre [R.L. Frank, E. Lenzmann, L. Silvestre, Uniqueness of radial solutions for the fractional Laplacian, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 69 (9) (2016) 1671-1726], showed similar uniqueness results for high dimensions ($N \geq 2$), in which they proposed a challenging open problem to extend their results about non-degeneracy and uniqueness of ground states to nonlinearities $f(u)$ beyond the pure-power case. In this paper, we aim to give an affirmative answer to this open issue for two classes of more general nonlinearities, including the case of sums of powers with certain conditions on exponents.

papers.title: Statistical Performance Guarantee for Subgroup Identification with Generic Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Across a wide array of disciplines, many researchers use machine learning (ML) algorithms to identify a subgroup of individuals who are likely to benefit from a treatment the most (``exceptional responders'') or those who are harmed by it. A common approach to this subgroup identification problem consists of two steps. First, researchers estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) using an ML algorithm. Next, they use the estimated CATE to select those individuals who are predicted to be most affected by the treatment, either positively or negatively. Unfortunately, CATE estimates are often biased and noisy. In addition, utilizing the same data to both identify a subgroup and estimate its group average treatment effect results in a multiple testing problem. To address these challenges, we develop uniform confidence bands for estimation of the group average treatment effect sorted by generic ML algorithm (GATES). Using these uniform confidence bands, researchers can identify, with a statistical guarantee, a subgroup whose GATES exceeds a certain effect size, regardless of how this effect size is chosen. The proposed methodology uses random treatment assignment, random sampling of units, and continuity and moment conditions, without requiring consistency or monotonicity of the ML score. We derive a Wiener representation of the estimation error, with corrections for the empirical subgroup threshold and the fixed treatment sample size. Estimating this representation gives asymptotically exact uniform coverage using Gaussian draws, without refitting the ML model. We also develop uniform bands for mean-adjusted treatment effects and other evaluation metrics. A simulation design and an application to a clinical trial of late-stage prostate cancer illustrate the subgroup identification problem.

papers.title: Dimension-8 SMEFT Matching Conditions for the Low-Energy Effective Field Theory
papers.abstract: In particle physics, the modern view is to categorize things in terms of effective field theories (EFTs). Above the weak scale, we have the SMEFT, formed when the heavy new physics (NP) is integrated out, and for which the Standard Model (SM) is the leading part. Below $M_W$, we have the LEFT (low-energy EFT), formed when the heavy SM particles ($W^\pm$, $Z^0$, $H$, $t$) are also integrated out. In order to determine how low-energy measurements depend on the underlying NP, it is necessary to compute the matching conditions of LEFT operators to SMEFT operators. These matching conditions have been worked out for all LEFT operators up to dimension 6 in terms of SMEFT operators up to dimension 6 at the one-loop level. However, this is not sufficient for all low-energy observables. In this paper we present the momentum-independent matching conditions of all such LEFT operators to SMEFT operators up to dimension 8 at tree level.

papers.title: Sharp spectral gap and large time asymptotics for the Poisson-Nernst-Planck system with confinement
papers.abstract: We study the Poisson--Nernst--Planck (Debye--Hückel) system for a single species of charged particles in $\mathbb R^d$, $d=2$ or $3$, with an external confinement potential. The particles repel each other through the Coulomb interaction. For a class of potentials with at least linear growth at infinity, solutions converge to the unique stationary state at an exponential rate in a weighted $\mathrm L^2$ space. The rate is given by the spectral gap of the linearized operator, which is symmetric for a scalar product adapted to the free energy. Our main result is that, for the harmonic potential $ϕ(x)=\frac\mu2\,|x|^2$, this spectral gap is exactly $μ$, for any mass and in both dimensions. The corresponding eigenspace is spanned by the translation modes. Unlike the attractive (Keller--Segel) case, the repulsive interaction destroys the monotonicity of the spectrum with respect to the angular momentum. We overcome this difficulty with a duality criterion and explicit \emph{chiral fluxes} built from vector spherical harmonics. These reduce the non-local spectral problem to one-dimensional weighted inequalities, which we prove by a ground state transform. The center of mass decays exactly like $e^{-μt}$. After removing this motion, the convergence rate improves to a second spectral gap $Λ_2>μ$, for which we prove an explicit lower bound in terms of the central density of the stationary state. As consequences, we obtain rates of convergence in $\mathrm L^p$ norms, and improved intermediate asymptotics for the unconfined system in $\mathbb R^2$, after recentering at the center of mass.

papers.title: Gate tunable spin splitting for Andreev spin qubits in Ge quantum well heterostructures
papers.abstract: Ge-based super-semi heterostructures are a promising platform for implementing Andreev spin qubits (ASQs). For example, they can be isotopically purified to eliminate nuclear spins that cause decoherence. However, spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which is a key ingredient for ASQs, is cubic in momentum for hole-based materials like Ge, in contrast with more-conventional ASQ materials (e.g., InAs wires), for which the SOC is linear in momentum. In this work, we study the interplay between geometrical properties like the channel width, and gate-tunable properties like the chemical potential, on ASQ operations. Intriguingly, we find that the spin splitting in a planar Ge Josephson junction does not depend on the junction width, in contrast with InAs nanowires. We explore the possibility of exploiting this property to suppress the harmful effects of charge traps. However, this prospect is spoiled by the fact that charge traps also affect the chemical potential, in addition to the channel width. Our results provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing spin splitting in ASQs and offer guidance for optimizing ASQs in other materials with cubic SOC.

papers.title: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases
papers.abstract: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves $.57$ micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.

papers.title: RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $π_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.

papers.title: Beyond the Sink Token: Sink-Guided Key Editing in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: In vision-language models (VLMs), a few sink tokens attract a disproportionate share of attention. While previous studies have examined why these tokens attract attention, we investigate how the sink-key direction affects attention to image and question tokens. Across four probed VLMs, boosting the magnitude of positive sink-aligned components increases attention on average, whereas boosting negative components decreases it; these responses persist through later layers. This identifies the native sink key as a reference for controlling attention beyond its own position. Motivated by this finding, we propose SHRINK, a training-free method that partially reduces sink-aligned components across visible keys during generation. On nine benchmarks under sampled reasoning, it improves mean accuracy by 5.1 and 2.7 percentage points on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with smaller gains on the other two main models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Gemma-3-4B. Beyond SHRINK, rescaling sink-aligned key components can replace the attention operations of two existing attention-steering methods, GIFT and ACG, with comparable accuracy on hallucination benchmarks.

papers.title: A multipurpose system of ordinary differential equations with exponential nonlinearity
papers.abstract: A system of ordinary differential equations (ODE) $\ddot{y}_k=\sum_{l=1}^n M_{kl}\exp y_l,~k=1,...,n$, where $M$ is an $n\times n$ nonsingular symmetric matrix, is discussed in detail. A two-parameter family of exact solutions is found and proved to be unstable for general $n$. A result of Adler and Moerbeke is shown to apply to our systems; it states that the only completely integrable cases of this system are equivalent to the Toda lattice with included non-nearest neighbour interactions. A few interesting applications are shown for some special $n$'s.

papers.title: Quantum resources and the onset of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem
papers.abstract: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.

papers.title: Trust the Ray, Not the Depth: Ray-Lateral Agreement for Multi-View 3D Human Pose Fusion
papers.abstract: Put a monocular mesh estimator behind every camera of a calibrated rig, and the reconstructed bodies land a meter or more apart. The cause is geometric: each estimate sits at the depth implied by a focal length the network assumed, not the one the camera has. Its error therefore points almost entirely along its own viewing ray, and the calibration tells us that direction exactly. To address this, we introduce the Ray-Lateral Agreement (RLA), which follows one rule: trust the ray, not the depth. RLA first slides every estimate along its own rays, which removes the depth bias and leaves the shape untouched. It then fuses the views one point at a time, under a Gaussian error whose precision follows each viewing ray. The maximum-likelihood solution is closed-form, interpolates between averaging and midpoint triangulation, and stays well conditioned where triangulation is singular. Robustness is the harder half, because correct views also disagree along their rays. Any weight built on the full residual therefore punishes good views together with bad ones. Ray-lateral agreement instead scores every view, at every point, by its residual across that view's own ray alone. We evaluated RLA on multi-camera public benchmark datasets. Across two, three, and four cameras and three per-view pose estimators, RLA consistently achieves lower worst-case error than all triangulation baselines.

papers.title: DexAttention: Distributed Sparse Attention through Rapid Online Planning and Persistent GPU Execution
papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces computation, but distributed execution may still transfer unnecessary data and incur substantial per-operation overhead. Mask-aware assignment and scheduling can reduce these costs, but replanning for dynamic masks must be cheaper than the execution time it saves. We present DexAttention, a distributed sparse attention system that co-designs fast online planning with persistent execution. Its assigner uses GPU-accelerated, topology-aware clustering to balance computational load and reduce communication. A lightweight greedy scheduler orders coarse communication and computation operations, while a persistent kernel on each GPU enforces fine-grained dependencies and dispatches ready tasks. This division keeps detailed synchronization out of planning while enabling overlap without repeated attention launches. The framework supports static and dynamic per-head masks across multiple attention compute kernels. On a four-node, 16-GPU cluster, DexAttention achieves a $1.39\times$ geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup over the fastest applicable baseline across 11 configurations. For dynamic video attention, it achieves $2.11$--$2.37\times$ speedups over Ring Attention including planning.

papers.title: Periodicity of Entire Solutions of $ff''=H^2$
papers.abstract: Let $f$ denote a transcendental entire function. The so called Yang's conjecture asserts that if for some integer $k$ ($\geq1$) the product $ff^{(k)}$ is periodic, then $f$ must be also periodic. In this paper, we prove that when $k=2$ for a given periodic transcendental entire function $H$, and $f$ is an entire solution of the equation $$ff''=H^2,$$ then \(f\) must be periodic.

papers.title: Real-space electrostatic sums through truncation error analysis
papers.abstract: Methods that treat electrostatics in real space, without explicit reciprocal-space evaluation, are appealing for large-scale atomistic simulations. They typically employ local charge-neutralization schemes, but their relationship to the underlying error contributions of the full Ewald sum has not been fully characterized. A principled basis for parameter selection is also lacking. In this work, we show that the correction terms of Wolf's and Pickard's real-space methods approximate the truncation error of real-space electrostatic sums. This perspective motivates simplified fixed-radii and force-shifted Pickard variants that preserve the truncation-error compensation behavior while enforcing continuity of pair energy and force at the cutoff. We derive a nonempirical scaling relation for the optimal path in the parameter space of the cutoff radius and screening distance, generalizing Pickard's empirical heuristic and explaining when and why it can fail. A systematic scheme for restoring omitted reciprocal contributions is introduced, which accelerates convergence to the full Ewald energy.

papers.title: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design
papers.abstract: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

papers.title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

papers.title: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security
papers.abstract: In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.

papers.title: The production of lepton pairs in heavy-ion collisions at SPS and RHIC energies
papers.abstract: We perform a quantitative study of dilepton production and elliptic flow in In+In collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=17.3$ GeV and isobar collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=200$ GeV, concentrating on the low and intermediate invariant mass regions. The medium evolution is simulated event-by-event with the multistage iEBE-MUSIC framework, and the electromagnetic emission combines for the first time quark-gluon plasma (QGP) emission calculated at next-to-leading order (NLO) in the strong coupling with in-medium radiation calculated with hadronic many-body theory. Freeze-out and surviving primordial $ρ$ decays are also included. The calculations are compared with the high-precision dimuon spectra measured by the NA60 Collaboration, and with STAR preliminary measurements of dielectron spectra and elliptic flow. We obtain effective temperatures extracted from the transverse-mass spectra, and we calculate the elliptic flow of the different dilepton sources. Our results suggest that dilepton measurements in the low-mass and high $p_T$ region can provide insight into higher-order corrections to the QGP emission rate.

papers.title: Degree and normalization frontiers for bounded QSVT inversion
papers.abstract: Quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) implements matrix inversion using bounded polynomials. Increasing polynomial degree can improve normalization and reduce amplified query cost, with savings that depend on the error criterion. However, existing bounded methods either fix the normalization or work far below the condition numbers of fault-tolerant resource estimates. We therefore analyze this trade-off for absolute reciprocal error, which controls inverse-operator accuracy, and for residual error, which suffices for normalized linear solves. For absolute reciprocal error, we establish a scaling limit to a constrained least-norm problem for entire functions and characterize its high-accuracy frontier using elliptic integrals. Constructions built from near-optimal limiting functions achieve certified query-cost savings over the rescaled minimax baseline of at least 11.8 percent at condition number ten thousand with error one millionth, and at least 22.8 percent at one million with error one ten-billionth. A simpler two-term rule also has certified savings, and its phase factors at condition number ten thousand pass numerical checks at selected points. For residual error, a sparse Chebyshev construction achieves certified savings over the residual-minimax baseline of at least 8.7 percent at condition number ten thousand with normalized-state error at most one hundred-millionth, and at least 13.1 percent at one million with error at most one ten-billionth. These results quantify the saving that a joint choice of degree and normalization gives beyond the minimax baselines.

papers.title: Profile Screening and Frequency-Secure Operating Limit Derivation for Data Center Microgrids
papers.abstract: Rapid power variations from artificial intelligence (AI) workloads pose frequency-security challenges for islanded data-center microgrids. This paper proposes a generator step- response-based framework to rapidly screen candidate load pro- files and derive frequency-secure operating limits for IT workload scheduling. Identified generator responses are superimposed to assess the cumulative frequency effects of successive load changes without repeated dynamic simulations. The framework identifies potentially unsafe intervals and determines allowable load magni- tudes, ramp rates, and minimum event spacing, while accounting for prediction uncertainty and governor limits. Validation on a 2.5 MVA islanded microgrid with eight generator configurations and 14 synthetic AI workload profiles shows that 94.75% of 40,208 assessment windows receive decisive screening labels, with no frequency-violating windows classified as secure.

papers.title: Electromagnetic Channel Model and Sensing Performance for ISAC: The Case of a Single Cylindrical Scatterer
papers.abstract: We propose an electromagnetic wireless channel model for accurate target localization in radar-like sensing scenarios. The model employs a self-consistent method grounded in wave scattering theory and imposing boundary conditions, providing the (impedance) channel transfer matrix for a propagation channel with a single target modeled as a cylindrical scatterer. The model is: 1) physics-based, as it includes electromagnetic interactions between objects; 2) unified, as it is valid in both near- and far-field regions. Within the canonical two-dimensional and 2.5-dimensional configurations with line-source and dipole-source excitations, respectively, the model supports dielectric cylinders with frequency-dependent permittivity. Localization accuracy is assessed via the Cramer-Rao lower bound for a dielectric cylinder with variable position, radius, and dielectric constant. Provisions for future extensions to extended targets are discussed in the context of 3GPP channel modeling.
