We check that it reconstructs full Lambda-Lemaitre-Tolman-Bondi profiles to numerical precision. We also provide a derivative-aware, cosmology-independent three-term symbolic fit that requires only the growth rate and the local and enclosed density contrasts. Across a representative set of matter-curvature-redshift combinations and for a shell located in the compensated transition, the maximum relative errors are 0.3% and 0.7% in the transverse and radial responses, respectively. This compact formulation separates the production of a density profile from its expansion response and makes the effect of radial gradients explicit.

papers.title: Inter-detector correlations in LIGO-Virgo strain: an exploratory study and possible astrophysical implications
papers.abstract: We investigate inter-detector correlations in public LIGO-Virgo strain around nine O2 and O3 events, using a band-pass-only statistic without waveform-template fitting. The primary sample comprises 27 event-pair measurements, with three complementary measurements for GW191127. Event-window maxima over $|τ|\leq35$ ms are compared with 200 surrounding off-source maxima. With verified fractional catalog epochs, seven of the 27 primary event-pair measurements, all H1$\times$L1, reach the local finite-background floor $p=1/201$. No individual comparison passes a Holm correction at 5% for this family; the available background limits the attainable tail resolution. Complementary comparisons of simultaneous and time-displaced off-source data show processing-dependent structure, including a local excess near GW200219 that does not recur at comparable size in the additional segments examined. We discuss the possibility that part of the strain classified operationally as noise contains an astrophysical contribution, including an accumulated gravitational-radiation background associated with Bondi radiative processes.

papers.title: Predicted Exotic Doubly Heavy-Strange Pentaquarks
papers.abstract: We predict exotic doubly heavy--strange pentaquarks with minimal quark content $u\bar d sQQ'$ ($QQ'=cc,bc,bb$) within a coupled-channel unitary framework where the interaction is derived from an extension of the local hidden gauge approach to the heavy-quark sector. We obtain a robust spectrum of manifestly exotic states; two states appear in the $u\bar d scc$ sector, three in $u\bar d scb$, and two in $u\bar d sbb$. These emerge either as bound states or resonances, along with seven additional virtual states manifested as threshold cusps. The binding mechanism is dominated by off-diagonal transitions among heavy-baryon--light-meson channels, while diagonal interactions are strongly suppressed. These results extend exotic hadron spectroscopy into the doubly heavy--strange sector and provide concrete targets for future experimental searches.

papers.title: Mechanics of heterogeneous fiber networks processed by an active fluid
papers.abstract: Internally generated active stresses can drive soft materials into structures that cannot form under thermal self assembly alone. For example, a microtubule-kinesin active fluid can assemble and irreversibly restructure actin-fascin networks. Increasing the motor concentration of the active fluid results in networks with broad pore size distribution and heterogeneous bundle structure. We probe the mechanics of these actively processed fiber networks by applying local forces with optical tweezers and measuring the strain response around the probe. Displacement fields of actively-processed networks propagate over a longer range than compared to unprocessed networks. Furthermore, networks processed at higher motor concentration are stiffer on average, while also exhibiting more heterogeneous response. At large strains, both unprocessed and actively processed networks exhibit strain softening and plastic restructuring. These measurements demonstrate that tunable active fluids can alter both the structure and viscoelastic properties of materials.

papers.title: Flat Space Physics from AdS Actions
papers.abstract: Flat spacetimes are foliated by hyperbolic slices that are geometrically three-dimensional de Sitter or anti-de Sitter spaces. As such, it is possible to construct flat space holographic dualities by applying the AdS/CFT bulk-to-boundary dictionary slice by slice. In this work, we reduce 4D actions for massless scalars in both Minkowski space and Klein space and massive scalars in Minkowski space to actions on these 3D dS and AdS slices. In both Minkowski and Klein space, the reduced theories have a continuous spectrum of fields originating from the reduction over the noncompact $x^2$ direction. These actions are linked by boundary terms arising from field configurations discontinuous across the lightcone. In the massless case, different asymptotic limits of the reduced field near the boundary of the unit hyperbolic slice replicate either lightcone or null infinity limits of the field; in the massive case, only one boundary mode of the reduced field has a simple geometric interpretation.

papers.title: Affine Supertrusses and Superbraces
papers.abstract: Brzeziński's trusses are ''ring-like'' algebraic structures in which the addition is replaced with an abelian heap operation and the binary product satisfies a natural distributivity rule over the ternary addition. This paper addresses the question of how to define affine super-versions of trusses. Taking our cue from the theory of algebraic supergroups, we define an affine supertruss as a representable functor from the category of unital associative supercommutative superalgebras to the category of trusses. The representing superalgebras are equipped with a ''cotruss'' structure-a new concept in itself. We show that from an affine supertruss, provided the binary product defines a supergroup, one can construct an affine two-sided superbrace, and so generalise Rump's braces to supermathematics. As an application of these constructions, we propose a generalisation of the set-theoretic Yang-Baxter equation to the setting of affine superschemes via a super-version of Adler's map.

papers.title: Low-Multiplicity Jets as Probes of GeV-Scale Light-Quark-Coupled Particles
papers.abstract: We propose a search at the LHC for GeV-scale particles coupling predominantly to light quarks based on low-multiplicity jets. The search targets production in association with a hard photon and uses the feature that a light gauge-singlet can only decay into a small number of hadronic channels, yielding jets with anomalously low charged-track multiplicity and mass compared to QCD jets at the same transverse momentum. We determine the sensitivity to scalar and pseudoscalar couplings to up-quarks, and suggest a data-driven estimate that reduces the sensitivity to jet modeling uncertainties. This search extends the reach to hadronically-coupled particles into a previously inaccessible regime.

papers.title: Distinct mechanisms underlying in-context learning in transformers
papers.abstract: Modern distributed networks, notably transformers, acquire a remarkable ability (termed `in-context learning') to adapt their computation to input statistics, such that a fixed network can be applied to data from a broad range of systems. Here, we provide a mechanistic characterization of this behavior in transformers trained on a finite set $S$ of discrete Markov chains. The transformer displays four algorithmic phases, characterized by whether the network memorizes or generalizes, and whether it uses 1-point or 2-point statistics. We show that the four phases are implemented by multi-layer subcircuits that exemplify two qualitatively distinct mechanisms for implementing context-adaptive computations. Minimal models isolate the key features of both motifs. Memorization and generalization phases are delineated by two boundaries that depend on data diversity, $K = |S|$. The first ($K_1^\ast$) is set by a kinetic competition between subcircuits and the second ($K_2^\ast$) is set by a representational bottleneck. A symmetry-constrained theory of a transformer's training dynamics explains the sharp transition from 1-point to 2-point generalization and identifies key features of the loss landscape that allow the network to generalize. Put together, we show that transformers develop distinct subcircuits to implement in-context learning and identify conditions that favor certain mechanisms over others.

papers.title: Min-Max Connected Multiway Cut
papers.abstract: We introduce a variant of the multiway cut that we call the min-max connected multiway cut. Given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and a set $Γ\subseteq V$ of $t$ terminals, partition $V$ into $t$ parts such that each part is connected and contains exactly one terminal; the objective is to minimize the maximum weight of the edges leaving any part of the partition. This problem is a natural modification of the standard multiway cut problem and it differs from it in two ways: first, the cost of a partition is defined to be the maximum size of the boundary of any part, as opposed to the sum of all boundaries, and second, the subgraph induced by each part is required to be connected. Although the modified objective function has been considered before in the literature under the name min-max multiway cut, the requirement on each component to be connected has not been studied as far as we know. Our main motivation for studying this problems is its close connection with the spanning tree congestion problem that has been extensively studied but on which little progress has been made. We show various hardness results for this problem, including a proof of weak NP-hardness of the weighted version of the problem on graphs with treewidth two, and $W[1]$-hardness for the problem when parameterized by the treewidth of the graph. Complementing our lower bounds tightly, we also provide a pseudopolynomial time algorithm as well as an FPTAS for the weighted problem on graphs of bounded treewidth. As a consequence of our investigation we also show that the (unconstrained) min-max multiway cut problem is NP-hard even for three terminals, strengthening the known results.

papers.title: TinyMyo: a Tiny Foundation Model for Flexible EMG Signal Processing at the Edge
papers.abstract: Objective: Surface electromyography (EMG) is widely used in biomechanics, rehabilitation, prosthetic control, and human-machine interfaces. Generalization across subjects, recording systems, and acquisition protocols remains challenging. Existing EMG foundation models (FMs) have limited support for multiple downstream tasks and deployment on low-power devices. Methods: We introduce TinyMyo, a 3.6-million-parameter Transformer encoder pre-trained on public EMG datasets using self-supervised masked reconstruction. TinyMyo supports multiple tasks with minimal changes to the task-specific prediction head. Results: We evaluated TinyMyo on hand gesture classification, hand kinematic regression, speech production, and speech recognition. For gesture classification, TinyMyo outperformed previously reported EMG FMs, achieving accuracies of 87.98% on NinaPro DB5, 97.1% on UCI-EMG, and 96.6% on EPN-612. On the GAP9 ultra-low-power microcontroller, TinyMyo achieved an inference time of 0.785 s and consumed 44.91 mJ per inference at an average power of 57.18 mW. A 1.9-million-parameter variant processed 5 s and 1 s input windows in 0.496 s and 0.089 s, respectively. Conclusion: TinyMyo demonstrates that a compact, self-supervised EMG encoder can support multiple downstream tasks and run on a low-power microcontroller. Significance: To our knowledge, this is the first deployment of an EMG FM on an ultra-low-power microcontroller, opening a path to on-device motor intent decoding, neuromuscular assessment, and human-machine interaction.

papers.title: EgoControl: Controllable Egocentric Video Generation via 3D Full-Body Poses
papers.abstract: Egocentric video generation with fine-grained control through body motion is a key requirement towards embodied AI agents that can simulate, predict, and plan actions. In this work, we propose EgoControl, a pose-controllable video diffusion model trained on egocentric data. We train a video prediction model to condition future frame generation on explicit 3D body pose sequences. To achieve precise motion control, we introduce a novel pose representation that captures both global camera dynamics and articulated body movements, and integrate it through a dedicated control mechanism within the diffusion process. Given a short sequence of observed frames and a sequence of target poses, EgoControl generates temporally coherent and visually realistic future frames that align with the provided pose control. Experimental results demonstrate that EgoControl produces high-quality, pose-consistent egocentric videos, paving the way toward controllable embodied video simulation and understanding.

papers.title: AI Behavioral Science: A Framework and Agenda
papers.abstract: We discuss the challenges and opportunities present in the rapidly emerging area of ``AI Behavioral Science.'' We frame it via three themes. First, as AI becomes ubiquitous and is increasingly proprietary and opaque, it becomes vital to develop models of AI and methods for assessing AI behavior. We outline how tools developed to assess people's behaviors by social scientists can be used to model, assess and infer AI's behaviors biases, tendencies, and heuristics. Second, we also discuss how AI can change the ways in which we learn about human behavior. Beyond its computational power, AI offers new techniques for simulating, inferring, predicting, and analyzing human behaviors. Third, as humans and AI are interacting in increasingly complex and intertwined systems, we need to analyze and model human-AI interactions including how human and AI behaviors depend on interactions at the individual level, how interacting systems of humans and AI behave, and ultimately how AI's integration into society affects economic and political outcomes. We discuss current research, questions, agendas, and goals in each of these three themes and how they depend upon each other.

papers.title: Concentration Inequalities for Branching Random Walks
papers.abstract: Motivated by phase transition problems in CSPs, we prove a more general concentration inequality that retains classical sub-Gaussian tails under a mild global linear-growth condition $|S_n| < Cn$, relaxing the bounded-increment assumption to finite exponential moments and requiring neither independence nor the martingale property. We further extend it to branching random walks (BRWs), obtaining the first concentration inequality for BRWs.

papers.title: Non-stationary wormholes with the presence of scalar fields and modified gravity
papers.abstract: Some novel regular spacetimes are considered that show a non-stationary wormhole structure. A Simpson-Visser-like procedure is applied to reconstruct these regular spacetimes, free of time-like and space-like singularities. Such a procedure is also applied to describe a regular cosmological expansion, where the universe reaches a minimum scale and then rebounds. This type of regular spacetime is achieved by considering some scalar fields as sources, with the appropriate kinetic term and scalar potential. We show that all these sources turn out to be ghosts due to the wrong sign of the kinetic term. These ghosts can, however, be eliminated by constraints. Nevertheless, the same procedure is also explored in the framework of modified gravities, particularly within the so-called f(R) gravity, where a new wormhole spacetime is also obtained that does not require a ghost scalar field.

papers.title: Information geometry and entanglement under phase-space deformation through nonsymplectic congruence transformation
papers.abstract: We investigate the relationship between Fisher-Rao (FR) information geometry and Gaussian quantum correlations under nonsymplectic phase-space transformations, with particular emphasis on noncommutative (NC) deformation implemented through the Bopp shift. Using the established affine invariance of the FR-metric, we examine the transformation properties of Gaussian covariance matrices and the positive partial transpose (PPT) criterion under invertible congruence transformations. For a bipartite Gaussian system, we demonstrate that keeping the canonical partial-transpose (PT) matrix fixed in the deformed phase space produces deformation-dependent spectral shifts that may cross the conventional PPT threshold. When the PT operation is transported together with the covariance and commutation matrices, the physical PPT spectrum and separability classification remain invariant under local Darboux transformations. We further investigate a two-dimensional anisotropic oscillator in NC phase space, where the deformation parameters modify the effective canonical Hamiltonian and consequently influence the Gaussian ground-state correlations and entanglement between canonical modes. The corresponding FR-geometry reveals that the original covariance manifold possesses constant negative scalar curvature. In contrast, the pure symmetric normal-form covariance family is intrinsically one-dimensional and flat. These results distinguish the statistical geometry of Gaussian covariance matrices from the physical quantum correlations determined by the Hamiltonian, commutation structure, and subsystem decomposition.

papers.title: Parameter-Specific Bias Diagnostics in Random-Effects Panel Data Models
papers.abstract: The Hausman specification test assesses the random-effects specification by comparing random-effects and fixed-effects estimators. This note uses the diagnostic of Karl and Zimmerman (2021) to give a coefficient-specific sensitivity summary from one fitted mixed model. The diagnostic measures alignment between fitted random effects and the weights used to estimate a coefficient or contrast. Its value need not equal finite-sample bias: fitted effects are shrunken, and response-dependent covariance estimates introduce an additional weighted-error term. We explain this distinction, describe simulations that refit the covariance parameters and retain the latent-effect and weighted-error contributions, and illustrate the calculations with gasoline-demand data and a multiple-membership value-added model. Connecting the diagnostic to established generalized least squares sensitivity analysis, including Vasnev's (2010) balanced-panel results, we identify it as the negative derivative of a coefficient or contrast with respect to the log scale of the random-effects covariance. With fitted covariance shapes held fixed, integrating the diagnostic over this log scale, upward from the fitted model, gives the random-effects estimate minus the fixed-effects estimate for a contrast estimable under both models. We also discuss conditioning on stochastic regressors and the additional assumptions needed for calibrated inference.

papers.title: Inequalities involving Higher Degree Polynomial Functions in $π(x)$
papers.abstract: Earlier research reflects that the two sides of Ramanujan's inequality for the prime-counting function \begin{align*} π(x)^2<\frac{ex}{\log x}π(x/e) \end{align*} happens to agree through four asymptotic orders. In this paper, we try to examine how this cancellation arises in higher-degree expressions and how shifts affect the size of the resulting gaps. In signed sums of equal powers of shifted prime counts, the first nonvanishing moment of the logarithmic shifts determines the leading term. A cubic comparison at five dilations exhibits four successive cancellations, leaving a gap of order $x^3/(\log x)^7$. A finite-difference argument proves its positivity for every real $x\geq e^{52}$ when the logarithmic shifts are spaced by $2$. When the shifts and nonnegative weights are fixed, the weighted Ramanujan gap retains order $x^2/(\log x)^6$. Its leading coefficient is $c^2(1+σ^2)$, where $c$ is the total rescaled weight and $σ^2$ is the weighted variance of the logarithmic shifts. We also give the explicit range $x\geq 85e$ for the logarithmically weighted five-shift inequality and determine the eventual sign of a polynomial family in every fixed integer degree $m\geq 3$. Exact counts and interval enclosures illustrate the expansions and the effect of variance at fixed rescaled weight and mean.

papers.title: A Primer on Zadoff Chu Sequences
papers.abstract: Zadoff-Chu (ZC) sequences are an important manifestation of spread spectrum in modern cellular systems, including LTE and 5G NR. They have to some extent displaced PN and Walsh sequences which were the mainstays of 3G cellular (WCDMA and cdma2000) and the 2G-era IS-95. ZC sequences are complex sequences with unit amplitude and particular phase shifts, as opposed to Walsh and PN codes which are real and binary valued, most commonly $\pm1$. ZC sequences have a number of remarkable and desirable properties that we define in the next section. Because of these properties, they are used for many key functions in current cellular systems, and are likely to be prevalent in future cellular systems as well. In LTE and 5G NR, they are widely used for a number of important initial access and overhead channel functions that are often overlooked by engineers who focus on data transmission. For example, ZC sequences are used for initial access in both the downlink (synchronization sequences) and uplink (random access premables). They are also used for transmitting uplink control information, and as pilot symbols for both uplink channel sounding and fine-grained channel estimation. It is not an exaggeration to say that most types of signals other than the data transmissions in modern cellular standards utilize ZC sequences. In this primer, we define ZC sequences and introduce their key properties, and provide some examples. We also discuss modified ZC sequences that are commonly used in practice, but are not, strictly speaking, ZC sequences. We also overview their uses in LTE and 5G.

papers.title: Difference-in-Differences Estimators for Treatments Continuously Distributed at Every Period
papers.abstract: When studying the effects of taxes, tariffs, or prices using panel data, the treatment is often continuously distributed in every period. We develop difference-in-differences (DID) estimators for such settings. We partition units into switchers, whose treatment changes between consecutive periods, and stayers, whose treatment remains constant. Under a parallel-trends assumption, we show that the slopes of switchers' potential outcomes with respect to the treatment are nonparametrically identified by DID comparisons between switchers and stayers sharing the same baseline treatment level. Conditioning on the baseline treatment is key, as it ensures that the underlying parallel-trends assumption accommodates time-varying treatment effects. We then study two weighted averages of these slopes, discuss their respective advantages, and propose for each a doubly robust, semiparametrically efficient, and $\sqrt{n}$-consistent estimator. Finally, we extend our framework to instrumental variables and illustrate it by estimating the effects of gasoline taxes on prices and fuel consumption.

papers.title: Waldspurger's formula via a prehomogeneous zeta integral on $F^2 \otimes \bigwedge^2 F^4$
papers.abstract: We give a new proof of Waldspurger's formula for toric periods of cuspidal automorphic forms on $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ over a number field, including the explicit constant. The proof compares two expansions of the residue at $s_0=1$ of a two-variable zeta integral on the twelve-dimensional prehomogeneous representation $F^2\otimes\bigwedge^2F^4$ of a parabolic subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_4\times\mathrm{GL}_2$, paired with an Eisenstein series induced from $π\boxtimesπ$. The first expansion, arising from the boundary geometry and the constant term of the Eisenstein series, identifies the residue with a Suzuki-Wakatsuki zeta integral; unfolding that integral along its generic orbits, whose connected stabilizers are tori, produces the square of the toric period. The second expansion, obtained by unfolding along a generic orbit whose stabilizer has identity component the diagonal $\mathrm{PGL}_2$, expresses the residue as the Petersson norm times an Euler product of local orbital integrals. Local residue identities at every place and an explicit computation of the unramified factors show that the two expressions share the same local factors; comparing them yields the formula, with the central $L$-value arising from the unramified computation.

papers.title: Unsupervised dense random survival forests identify interpretable patient profiles with heterogeneous treatment benefit
papers.abstract: Precision oncology seeks to match patients with treatments that maximize clinical benefit. Identifying clinically interpretable subgroups with differential treatment effects from randomized clinical trials, however, remains challenging. We propose a subgroup-discovery framework based on dense random survival forests, with a splitting criterion that combines prognostic discrimination and treatment-effect heterogeneity. The framework aggregates patient proximity matrices across multiple forest configurations, identifies subgroups using the resulting treatment-informed similarity representation, and summarizes them through concise covariate rules. An empirical calibration procedure assesses evidence for treatment-effect heterogeneity. Extensive simulations demonstrate the ability of the framework to distinguish heterogeneous from homogeneous treatment-effect settings and recover treatment-responsive subgroups, with empirical Type I error control under the homogeneous scenarios considered. An application to a Phase III oncology trial identifies a treatment-responsive patient profile defined by baseline characteristics, illustrating the potential of the framework to inform subgroup-focused clinical research and future trial design.

papers.title: Fast Inference-Time Policy Refinement via Action-Affine World Models
papers.abstract: Imitation policies can fail through compounding errors, while existing refinement methods often require additional on-policy learning or expensive online planning. Our key insight is to model the response to small corrections around a policy proposal in an affine form that enables fast optimization. We refine a frozen imitation policy using an \textit{action-affine world model} (A\textsuperscript{2}WM), trained offline from perturbed policy rollouts. Conditioned on history and the proposal, the model directly predicts a nominal trajectory and a linear action response over the full horizon. With quadratic costs and linear constraints, refinement becomes a cheap quadratic program (QP), requiring only one model evaluation and one QP solve per control step. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to combine an action-affine world model with QP-based inference-time refinement of frozen imitation policies. Across four manipulation tasks, our framework achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines, adding only 4.2 ms of mean refinement latency per control step, excluding base-policy sampling.

papers.title: Forecasting Retail Sales at Every Grain: Trees, Foundation Models, Transformers and World Models Compared on Four Public Data Sets
papers.abstract: A retailer makes decisions from the same demand at different grains: store orders by item and day, promotions by item and week, category reviews and supplier terms. This paper asks whether one forecast, built at the finest grain and summed to every coarser grain, can serve them all, and which model does that best. It compares LightGBM, pretrained foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos-Bolt, Timestral), the Temporal Fusion Transformer and a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, on M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat and Corporacion Favorita, with the world model and LightGBM tuned by a common search. When to use the average: the average of the tuned world model and LightGBM, summed to every grain, has the lowest error in 22 of 27 grain and data set cases and is never the least accurate on the final held-out periods. When to use the world model: on existing items kept out of training it loses at most 0.040 in scaled error, against up to 0.311 for LightGBM, and on lines with short history it is clearly more accurate on six of nine data sets. When to use LightGBM: on heavily promoted lines, fast sellers and lines with long history (six of nine data sets each) and in price-cut weeks. Inconclusive: lines never promoted and slow lines are close to even, and 52 weeks ahead the average is the most accurate on five of seven data sets, with the world model ahead of LightGBM on two of seven. The findings hold for these data sets and the price and promotion levers; anyone adopting them should rerun every comparison on their own data.

papers.title: A Threshold-Free Visual-Semantic Matching Metric for Evaluating Consistency in Subject-Driven Image Generation
papers.abstract: We propose a Threshold-Free Visual-Sematic Matching (TF-VSM) metric, to quantitatively evaluate localized visual consistency across varying poses and environments in subject-driven text-to-image generation. TF-VSM is a fully continuous, threshold-free visual consistency metric paired with an extended feature-disentanglement retraining schedule for dual-branch ResNet feature-aggregation networks. Existing metrics suffer from point-alignment dropouts, threshold sensitivity, and score instability. To address them, our TF-VSM, rather than enforcing rigid binary cutoffs ($T_s$, $T_v$), weights every object point by a non-linear semantic match confidence $w_j = ReLU(\hat s_j)^2$ to yield a closed-form confidence-weighted score without any hand-tuned hyperparameters. Experimental results show that, TF-VSM attains Pearson 0.638 and Spearman 0.674 oracle correlation, improving over the pretrained VSM baseline (0.454/0.589) by +0.171/ + 0.116 after retraining, and drastically outperforming CLIP (-0.052/ -0.004), DINO (0.087/0.121), and VLMs (0.096/0.003). Six diagnostic ablations confirm that smooth confidence weighting is the right mechanism, that hard semantic gating is brittle (dropping to 0.533 Pearson at $T_s$=0.8), and that the threshold-free metric is essentially invariant to the training time loss balance $α$. Code is available at: https://github.com/bwshan/TF-VSM.

papers.title: Asymptotic Order of the Minimum Number of Graph-Saturating Edges I
papers.abstract: Given an $H$-free graph $G$, a non-edge $e$ of $G$ is called $H$-saturating if $G+e$ contains a copy of $H$. The function $f_H(n,m)$ denotes the minimum number of $H$-saturating non-edges over all $n$-vertex $H$-free graphs with exactly $m$ edges. In this paper, we fully characterize the asymptotic order of $f_H(n,\operatorname{ex}(n,R)+1)$ for any fixed graph $H$ with $χ(H)\ge χ(R)$, where $R$ is any fixed edge-critical graph, and resolve the conjecture proposed by He et al. (J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 159 (2023), 42-60).

papers.title: TIVS: Mapping the Sensitivity Landscape of Visual Token Transformations in MLLMs
papers.abstract: Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have explored visual token pruning, quantization, and feature compression. However, the properties that determine whether transformed visual tokens remain usable by a frozen decoder are not well characterized. We introduce \textbf{TIVS (Token Identity Versus Statistics)}, a training-free intervention framework that separately studies sequence permutation, token retention, numerical precision, and statistical replacement under controlled conditions. On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations change TinyLLaVA accuracy by only $-0.17$ percentage points on average, while changing 4.69\% of individual predictions. Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements decrease accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points on the same subset. Further experiments with exact moment constraints, quantization error, token retention, and additional visual tasks reveal how strongly the effects depend on the original feature values and the evaluation setting. These findings provide an empirical basis for assessing visual token transformations in frozen MLLMs and designing more reliable multimodal interfaces.

papers.title: Analysis choices can produce apparent rich-club differences: an Alzheimer's disease EEG case study
papers.abstract: Background: The weighted rich-club coefficient tests whether a network's most strongly connected nodes are preferentially interconnected. Its interpretation depends on two often-implicit choices: how the randomised comparison networks are constructed, and whether the hubs are re-identified in each comparison network or held fixed at those of the observed network. When hubs are defined by connection strength, these choices change what the coefficient tests. New method: We examined how these choices affect inference using resting-state EEG from 20 people with Alzheimer's disease and 20 controls. Holding the data fixed, we compared four analysis pipelines, crossing two ways of building the comparison networks (global weight reshuffle or strength-conditioned null) with the two hub choices, and ran a calibration study using data constructed to contain no preferential hub coupling beyond nodal strength. Results: An apparent eyes-open group difference in rich-club organisation appeared only under the pipeline combining a global weight reshuffle with re-identified hubs. Under the empirical resampling ensemble, that pipeline reported a group difference in 43% of pseudo-studies, always higher in the Alzheimer's disease group, while the other three stayed near the expected 5%. Comparison with existing methods: Unlike global weight reshuffling, strength-conditioned nulls approximately preserve nodal strengths; fixing observed hubs also retains the identity of the core being tested. Conclusions: The same data can support or dissolve an apparent rich-club difference depending on these choices. No single choice is universally correct, but reporting which were made, and why they fit the question being asked, is essential to interpreting the result.

papers.title: Decorated lattices: hyperuniformity and limit theorems
papers.abstract: We introduce \emph{decorated lattices}, a point process obtained by placing finite random point configurations in lattice cells. A stationary mark field selects the motif laws and acts as a random environment transmitting dependence between cells, while allowing flexible local arrangements. Using this construction, one can efficiently generate large regions of disordered patterns with desired local behavior while the random environment controls the asymptotic density fluctuations. Under moment and summability assumptions, we derive an explicit decomposition of the Bartlett spectral measure into contributions from conditional motif fluctuations and correlations between marks. This yields criteria for hyperuniformity, or generally $p$-uniformity. Independent, nondegenerate count fluctuations destroy hyperuniformity, whereas suitable dependence governed by the random environment can restore it despite random and unequal cell counts. Once count fluctuations are sufficiently suppressed, motif geometry and its spatial correlations govern the finer order of uniformity. Under mixing assumptions, we also establish central limit theorems for linear statistics, with fluctuations governed by cell counts or, at a finer scale, by the first spatial moments of the motifs.

papers.title: Can AI Judge You? An Empirical Audit of Deployment Readiness in LLM-assisted Hiring Systems
papers.abstract: Delegating resume screening to large language models (LLMs) requires organizations to establish whether they can distinguish candidates by relevant qualifications while allowing only authorized users to change screening rules or approve exceptions. To this end, we develop a system architecture that separates candidate evidence, evaluation, permission controls, and assessment record, and empirically examine two complementary dimensions of its deployment readiness. First, we assess its operational readiness on four LLMs using a controlled experiment on 210 resumes across 14 job roles and six decision interfaces. Second, we assess its compliance readiness by testing how it handles unauthorized user requests and instructions embedded in resumes. We find that operational performance depends on the choice of evaluation interface: scalar scores generally distinguish qualification changes better than simple pass/fail judgments, while comparative judgments are sensitive to presentation order. Explicit permission rules and separation of resume content from instructions reduce unauthorized compliance, to a varying degree of effectiveness across LLMs and usage contexts. Finally, we find that LLM evaluators often diverge between their decisions and offered justifications. Going beyond simply evaluating LLMs for hiring tasks, our framework supports an audit of a fully configured resume evaluation system to enable its deployment decision.

papers.title: Latent World Modeling for Point-Cloud Video Pretraining
papers.abstract: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/InitalZ/PointWM.

papers.title: The topological degree of the regular $SU(3)$ Toda system
papers.abstract: We resolve the long-standing open problem of computing the Leray--Schauder degree of the regular $SU(3)$ Toda system on a closed oriented surface $M$. If $d_{m,k}$ denotes the degree in the block $(4πm,4π(m+1))\times(4πk,4π(k+1))$, then \[ \sum_{m,k\geq0}d_{m,k}x^my^k =(1-x)^{χ(M)-1}(1-y)^{χ(M)-1}(1-xy)^{χ(M)}, \] where $χ(M)$ is the Euler characteristic of $M$. Nonvanishing of $d_{m,k}$ thus gives an existence criterion in terms of the topology of $M$ and the parameter block. At each step of the degree computation, we show that the only possible local mass pairs are $(4π,0)$ and $(8π,4π)$. We use generic perturbations and local second-order information on the weights to exclude collisions of shadow centers and splitting at mixed blow-up points. The shadow degrees and the Morse index then give the degree jump at each critical value.

papers.title: What Matters for Cross-Modal Alignment
papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different modalities converge toward a shared representation. Related work aligns frozen image and text encoders on natural images without paired data. We test zero-pair alignment on five datasets across four modalities: natural images, environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D computed tomography (CT). It succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four. We analyze the failures and find that alignment must first locate the subspace where the modalities co-vary and then orient the mapping within it. Consistent with previous studies, medical imaging is the hardest case: its shared subspace carries the smallest fraction of the variance. When this fraction is small, alignment needs image-text pairs, and random-matrix theory predicts how many pairs are needed. These findings motivate LightAlign: a few pairs let a ridge regression between two frozen encoders locate and orient the mapping simultaneously, and a classifier fitted only on report text then predicts findings from the mapped images. On 3D CT, LightAlign surpasses models trained end to end on image-report pairs without finding-level labels: with only 200 pairs, LightAlign outperforms CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (0.754 vs. 0.733 AUROC), and with only 100 CT-RATE pairs, it does so on RAD-ChestCT, an out-of-distribution dataset from a different hospital. On CheXpert, it reaches 0.862 mean AUROC with only about 5% as many pairs as models trained on MIMIC-CXR.

papers.title: Subwavelength resonances and localization in finite resonator chains with a size defect
papers.abstract: We study subwavelength resonances of a finite chain of $N\ge2$ close-to-touching spherical resonators in three dimensions with a single radius defect of relative size $τ\in(0,1]$ and gap width $\varepsilon$. Taking the high-contrast limit before the narrow-gap limit, we prove that the positive generalized eigenvalues of the weighted chain coupling matrix with respect to the volume matrix determine the leading relative resonant frequencies. After eliminating the finite tails, we obtain an exact characteristic determinant and identify a unique critical ratio $τ_*\in(0,1)$ at which the largest eigenvalue crosses the upper edge of the homogeneous recurrence band $[0,4]$. For every $0<τ<τ_*$, exactly one eigenvalue lies above this band, and its eigenvector decays geometrically along the tails. As $τ\toτ_*^-$, its recurrence decay length diverges like $(τ_*-τ)^{-1/2}$. As $τ\to0$, exactly one eigenvalue diverges like $τ^{-2}$ and its eigenvector concentrates at the defect; if the defect is interior, one additional positive eigenvalue has order $τ$. For suitably normalized relative resonant modes, the sequential limit of the $\varepsilon$-scaled gradient supremum in each gap equals the absolute difference between adjacent reduced amplitudes. For the largest-eigenvalue mode, this yields defect-adjacent gradient concentration as the defect shrinks.

papers.title: Giant Raman Optical Activity in Chiral and Polar Ni$_3$TeO$_6$
papers.abstract: Raman optical activity (ROA) measures the difference in Raman scattering intensity for right- and left-circularly polarized light and reflects the chirality of excitations. In solids, ROA is commonly very weak. For the phonons of chiral and polar Ni$_3$TeO$_6$, we find a giant ROA with magnitude 100 times higher than commonly reported for molecules. The systematic analysis based on phonon selection rules allows the chiral and achiral scattering channels to be separated. First-principles calculations of the Raman tensor at finite phonon momentum relate the effect to the phonon modulation of the band-geometric and band-dispersion contributions to optical gyrotropy. This establishes Raman optical activity as a probe of electron--phonon modulation of the band geometry in an insulator.

papers.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We formalize item-level preference distillation on the SID prefix tree, deriving an exact factorization of item preference distributions into prefix conditionals and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into conditional KL terms. Guided by this decomposition, we renormalize the generator's probabilities over legal next tokens and match the resulting distributions to the teacher's conditional preferences along the ground-truth SID path, jointly optimizing the distillation objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation and demonstrate that REGER consistently outperforms existing GR baselines while retaining efficient inference.

papers.title: On complemented skew braces
papers.abstract: We investigate complemented skew left braces, that is, skew braces in which every skew subbrace admits a complement. We establish that if every minimal subbrace of a finite skew brace is complemented, then the brace is supersoluble and all its skew subbraces of prime power order are elementary abelian. We also show that the converse does not hold in general, providing a finite counterexample. Furthermore, we prove that every subbrace of a finite direct product of square-free skew braces is complemented. Finally, we extend our investigation to the infinite setting, proving that every multipermutational complemented skew brace is hypercyclic and that all its skew subbraces whose additive groups are $p$-groups are elementary abelian.

papers.title: Local limit theorem for branching processes with immigration
papers.abstract: Let $\{Y_{n}, n\geq 0\}$ be a critical branching process with immigration. Under the minimal moment restrictions, namely, assuming finite variance for the number of particles of the offspring and finite mean for the number of immigrating particles, we obtain a local limit theorem for the process $\{Y_{n}\}$.

papers.title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
papers.abstract: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

papers.title: Uniqueness and Nondegeneracy of Positive Bounded Solutions for Semilinear Dirichlet Problems in Exterior-Star Domains
papers.abstract: We prove the uniqueness and nondegeneracy of positive bounded solutions for the Dirichlet problem $$-Δu=f(u)\,\ \ \text{in}\ \ Ω, \ \ u=0\,\ \ \text{on}\ \ \partialΩ,$$ where $f$ is a positive reaction and $Ω\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^d$ is a uniformly $C^{2,γ}$ domain with a star-shaped complement. Our uniqueness result gives a positive answer to Open Question 1 of [H. Berestycki and C. Graham, ARMA, 2026].

papers.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

papers.title: Repairing actuator schedules under graph constraints
papers.abstract: We consider a discrete-time linear system in which each actuator is assigned to one time slot. A graph $H$ records which pairs of actuators cannot share a slot. We seek to remove conflicts by exchanging actuators between slots, while preserving all tail reachability spaces. These spaces describe the terminal corrections available from each time slot onward. We give a sufficient condition based on the number of exchanges that preserve the required bases. The condition guarantees repair from every compatible starting schedule. Two bounds for checking it use failed basis tests and dependent column selections. Each accepted exchange reduces the conflict count, so the procedure uses at most as many exchanges as there are initial conflicts. An explicit family with unequal rank increments admits repair when $3N>4Δ(H)+4$, where $Δ(H)$ is the largest number of forbidden partners of any actuator. We also give a family of two-slot examples with only one forbidden partner per actuator and two initial conflicts. The basis constraints force every strict improvement to move arbitrarily many actuators, although one exchange suffices without those constraints. A second example has a connected conflict graph and one initial conflict.

papers.title: B-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs
papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/ZevineXu/B-OPSD

papers.title: Classification problems for diassociative and dendriform algebras: a survey
papers.abstract: Diassociative algebras (associative dialgebras) and dendriform algebras are vector spaces with two binary operations, introduced by J.-L. Loday in the study of Leibniz algebras; their operads are Koszul dual to each other. We survey the classification problem for these two classes, including the Zinbiel algebras, the commutative dendriform algebras, which are Koszul dual to Leibniz algebras. We recall the definitions, the main examples and the Loday diagram with its extension by left-symmetric algebras and dialgebras, and describe the methods used to classify algebras of small dimension: direct computation from lists of associative algebras, annihilator (central) extensions and geometric classification by degenerations. We then collect, by dimension, the known algebraic classifications of diassociative algebras, dendriform algebras and their commutative case, the Zinbiel algebras, point out lists that later work corrected, and summarise the cohomological results that the methods rely on. We close with a list of open problems.

papers.title: A Multigrid Finite State Projection Algorithm For The Solution Of The Reaction-Diffusion Master Equation
papers.abstract: We develop a multigrid method for the finite state projection of the reaction-diffusion master equation (RDME). The RDME evolves the joint probabilities of molecular count configurations across well-mixed voxels coupled by local reactions and diffusive jumps. When fast diffusion or large reaction rates make this evolution stiff over long time horizons, implicit time stepping requires solving a large shifted linear system at every step. Grouping neighboring voxels and summing their molecular counts produces a hierarchy of coarser state spaces terminating at a one-voxel chemical master equation. Restriction sums residual entries with the same coarse counts, while multinomial prolongation preserves the RDME generator form on every level with explicit coarse reaction and diffusion rates. For reversible diffusion, the error omitted by coarsening is bounded by the graph Dirichlet energy of jumps inside the aggregates, with a constant independent of population. Numerical tests with standard multigrid cycles and point or block Gauss-Seidel smoothing reach 7.16 million states and resolve rare probabilities of order $10^{-7}$.

papers.title: Weight-Space Programming for Materials Science
papers.abstract: A materials discovery campaign often begins with almost no measurements of the property it is searching for, and the models that rank candidates or screen the output of a generator then have to be built from those first few labels. Following recent work on weight-space programming, in which a language model writes the weights of a small network directly as text, we show that a general-purpose model, given the task in words, the names of the inputs and a network of 16 hidden units with every weight set to zero, can provide this starting point by filling in all of the weights from what it has learned about materials. With no labels, the networks of the strongest model rank experimental alloys at Spearman co-efficient = 0.64 to 0.79, where the best of five simple descriptors reaches 0.47 to 0.62. They rank the bulk modulus of crystals added during generative discovery loops at 0.95, where the inverse volume per atom reaches 0.89, and 35 phase-equilibrium targets computed with Thermo-Calc at a mean of 0.67, close to the 0.70 of an extrapolation from calculated binary and ternary data. As the prior mean of a Gaussian process they raise the ranking at five labels from 0.35 to 0.69 on alloys and from 0.15 to 0.95 on crystals, and they lower the regret of Bayesian optimization significantly on 4 of 5 experimental tasks and on 13 to 16 of 33 computed targets, depending on how multiple tests are corrected, without raising it significantly on any. The same networks also serve as the mean of a Bayesian neural network and as a screen for the samples of two crystal generators, where they do as well as standard models trained on 400 labeled structures. The gain is confined to the first tens of labels and to targets that no rule or sub-system extrapolation already ranks.

papers.title: Theoretical Instability Models of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions
papers.abstract: The nature of the Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPE) is still not firmly established while the phenomenon probes the innermost part of the accretion flow undergoing dramatic changes. In this chapter we review the possibility that the observed rapid variability is caused by the accretion disk instability. We summarise the defining observational properties of QPE sources: time scales of recurrence, the amplitudes of soft X-ray flares, high coherence over many cycles, and comparatively modest time-averaged luminosities. We then translate these into constraints on the characteristic radius, accretion rate, and energy reservoir of the inner disk. We review the main classes of disk instabilities relevant to supermassive black holes: radiation pressure induced thermal/viscous limit cycles, magnetically mediated inner disk transitions, and coupling to disk winds that can produce the oscillatory behavior. For each scenario we discuss the required parameter space (black hole mass, Eddington ratio, viscosity prescription, and truncation radius), the predicted spectral and timing signatures, and the degree of fine tuning needed to reproduce the observed duty cycles and flare morphologies. We highlight key tensions, including the extremely soft spectra, short recurrence times compared with standard viscous times at tens of gravitational radii, and the weak or absent contemporaneous optical/UV variability in several systems. Finally, we outline observational tests that may help distinguish between instability driven and geometrical or orbital models: phase resolved spectroscopy to track the temperature evolution, searches for hysteresis in hardness-intensity diagrams, reverberation and absorption variability tied to winds, and long baseline monitoring to measure drift in period and energy output.

papers.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Distribution System Load Restoration
papers.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

papers.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
papers.abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

papers.title: Structural functional identifiability of unknown differential equation observation maps
papers.abstract: In many differential equation models of real-world systems, the mechanistic structure of the dynamics is known, but the map from the dynamics to the observations is not. This is potentially problematic, as it can prevent us from e.g. learning model parameter values from data. Examples where this occurs include measuring a fluorescent marker as a proxy for the dynamics of a cellular circuit, and using wastewater measurements to follow the development of an epidemic. The nascent field of hybrid modelling, in which machine learning components (like neural networks) are embedded within mechanistic models, provides the tools to learn such maps. Here, the system's dynamics keep their mechanistic form, while a neural network represents the unknown observation map and is trained alongside any unknown core system parameters. This raises a question of identifiability: when can the true observation map be learnt, and when does one simply learn some map that transforms the dynamics into the available data? Building on previous work, we show how structural functional identifiability analysis can establish whether a model's unknown observation maps and core system parameters are identifiable, i.e. can be uniquely learnt from data. We both prove general results on when models with unknown observation maps are, and are not, identifiable, and demonstrate a general methodology (based on differential algebra) for assessing the identifiability of such models. This paves the way for applying classic differential equation workflows to the many real-world systems that contain such unknown maps.

papers.title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
papers.abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.

papers.title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media
papers.abstract: A field theory is presented for predicting damage and fracture in brittle materials. Four concepts are used: a new nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis in anisotropic media, a new type of phase field coming from a constitutive law, the evolution of material displacement from Newton's second law, and a new incorporation of scaled strength surfaces into constitutive laws for predicting dynamic and quasi-static fracture patterns. The elastic softening is governed by the strain dynamics through the constitutive law and in this way we provide the two way coupling between strain and fracture. Simulations validating the approach for both dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis are compared to experimental results and other simulation methods. The model is capable of predicting material strength in titania and the competition between strength and energy in soda lime glass and titana and captures dynamic crack branching in soda lime glass and concrete.

papers.title: Perfect matching complexes of antiprism graphs and independence complexes of generalized Petersen graphs $GP(n,2)$
papers.abstract: We show that the perfect matching complexes of antiprism graphs and the independence complexes of the generalized Petersen graphs $GP(n, 2)$ are homotopy equivalent to wedges of spheres, and we determine the number and dimensions of the spheres. For the former we compute the initial values of Adamaszek's recursion for the independence complexes of cubes of cycles.

papers.title: A mechanistic characterization of missingness at random
papers.abstract: The missingness-at-random (MAR) assumption underlying many missing-data methods describes abstract statistical independences, whereas practitioners reason more naturally about the causal mechanisms that generate missingness. To bridge this gap, we provide a mechanistic characterization of MAR in terms of paths in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) modified to allow certain edges to cease to operate when an incomplete variable is missing, a property termed "context-specific causal irrelevance (CSCI)". Under a faithfulness condition, MAR holds if and only if the modified DAG contains no MAR-violating paths. Without CSCI, this condition reduces to a previously established d-separation condition, VMAR; thus, MAR without VMAR requires specific kinds of CSCI, as can occur with monotone dropout. These results shift the burden on investigators from passively invoking MAR to justifying, on substantive grounds, the specific mechanisms it requires. We then consider identification of a target law p(v) of variables V by a MAR-assuming analysis, e.g., multiple imputation, that includes complete auxiliary variables Z (variables not in V). Barring a perfect cancellation, such an analysis recovers p(v) if and only if MAR holds with respect to V and Z jointly. We show that if there exists any set of auxiliaries such that (V, Z) obeys MAR, then the complete candidate auxiliaries that are ancestors of the target variables or their missingness indicators form a sufficient set. Contrary to standard recommendations, not all candidate auxiliaries should be used: even complete auxiliaries can introduce MAR violations that would not otherwise occur. We illustrate these results with simulations and an analysis of sexual identity change in the Stockholm Public Health Cohort, where our results indicate that a candidate auxiliary, income, should be excluded; including it attenuated estimates toward the null.

papers.title: Single-Vertex Metropolis on Minor-Free Graphs: A General EPTAS
papers.abstract: We consider a class of combinatorial optimization problems where the goal is to find a largest induced subgraph with a prescribed property. We assume that the property is preserved by taking induced subgraphs and disjoint unions, holds for all edgeless graphs, and can be tested in polynomial time. We study the single-vertex Metropolis process for this class of problems. We show that on graphs excluding an arbitrary fixed minor $H$, this process is a randomized efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme. Starting from any feasible solution on a graph with $n$ vertices, it finds a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation within $\exp(O_H(\varepsilon^{-2})) n(n+\log(1/δ))$ steps with probability at least $1-δ$. This includes maximum independent set, maximum induced forest, maximum induced bipartite subgraph, and maximum induced subgraph of degree at most one. The proof uses improving exchanges on one fixed division of the input graph into regions. A recursive separator construction performs each exchange inside a region of size $r$ in at most $2r$ moves, with temporary loss $O_H(\sqrt r)$. We count move sequences through each transition and bound the probability of avoiding all near-optimal states. The general theorem bounds the number of Metropolis steps in terms of the temporary loss along improvement paths. We extend the result to bounded weight imbalance and give a weighted-star obstruction for unrestricted weights.

papers.title: An AI-Based OSSE Framework to Evaluate Learned Physical Consistency: A Multi-Model Study Using FourCastNet, Aurora, Prithvi WxC, and GraphCast
papers.abstract: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) are a central methodology for evaluating future atmospheric observing systems. We present the first AI-based OSSE framework to test whether different AI weather models can reproduce comparable physical impact from new observations that traditional physics based models generate. We evaluate four distinct architectural AI models on the Charney conjecture that incomplete historical observations can infer the present state of the atmospheric. We considner- FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora and Prithvi WxC and integrate each autoregressively over a 60-day forecast horizon. After a 30-day spin-up, we insert ERA5 temperature fields to infer winds and related atmospheric fields. Similar OSSE experiments are conducted for wind insertion. We measure the performance of each model's response to observational information on a 30-day data assimilation cycle forecast with and without data insertion. Distinct architectural AI weather models respond differently to the same OSSE observations. Foundation models (i.e. Prithvi WxC and Aurora), produce the strongest impact. For example, while GraphCast is the weakest, all three of the four models capture the temperature-to-geopotential height response. The two foundational models retain a positive, non-trivial, tropical zonal wind at 500 hPa response to temperature insertion. Various data insertion experiments can vary significantly even within a given architecture. We identify an architecture-specific numerical instability in GraphCast's full 37-level configuration that produces a runaway feedback concentrated at the uppermost levels with ERA5 temperature insertion correctable by excluding levels at or below 100 hPa.

papers.title: Causal Input--Output Modeling with Prior Information
papers.abstract: We study the problem of inferring a causal input--output model from unpaired marginal observations and a given prior coupling. We formulate this problem using entropic causal optimal transport, which seeks a coupling that preserves the observed marginals, satisfies a one--sided causality constraint, and remains close to the prior. For Gaussian marginals and general quadratic costs, we prove that the optimal coupling is Gaussian and reduce the problem to a finite--dimensional optimization over covariance matrices. Using a Cholesky transformation to simplify the causality constraint, we derive a Lagrangian dual formulation and develop a block coordinate descent algorithm with explicit update formulas. We establish linear convergence of the algorithm, with explicit convergence rates, and prove stability of the optimal coupling under marginal covariance perturbations and derive a statistical error bound. We further show its equivalence to Sinkhorn iterations. Numerical experiments demonstrate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and illustrate the predictive advantages of causal couplings.

papers.title: New necessary conditions on $h$-vectors of simplicial balls
papers.abstract: Although the $h$-vectors of simplicial balls of dimension at most $4$ have been completely characterized, much less is known in dimensions $5$ and higher. We establish new necessary conditions on the $h$-vectors of simplicial balls in these dimensions. Together with the necessary conditions of Billera and Lee and the sufficient conditions of Kolins, our results yield a complete characterization of the $h$-vectors of $5$- and $6$-dimensional simplicial balls. We also give a characterization of $h$-vectors of simplicial balls of any dimension with neighborly boundary.

papers.title: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact
papers.abstract: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text, and the strongest published checkers are single models. We describe GauntletScore, an evidence engine whose few rules and thresholds were set on the benchmark's development split. It puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers and records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. It combines the measurements with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), following the leaderboard's approach, GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy, above every average published on the leaderboard as of 15 November 2026. That places it level with the best of them, nimble-v4-max (79.45 from its published dataset scores; the engine's 95% interval, 78.47 to 80.53, contains it). On the same claims it beats two of its three readers used alone (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points (95% intervals 0.80 to 2.53 and 1.29 to 3.06). Without AggreFact-CNN, described below, the leads are 0.90 and 1.32 and both intervals stay above zero. The engine also records the evidence behind every verdict, which a single model does not. Its largest margin is on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format that resembles much regulated writing. There it scores 76.45, the best on the leaderboard, against 70.1 for the next best and 63.9 to 67.8 for the six systems with the highest averages. The test split was run once, on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. We release per-claim predictions and the scoring script.

papers.title: BATMoS: Budget-Aware Guidance Allocation for Efficient Video Diffusion
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of a video diffusion model's inference budget depends on where computation is spent along the denoising trajectory. Across eight equal-budget inference configurations, VBench total scores span 4.80 points, highlighting the importance of explicit allocation design. Our key insight is that guidance evaluations are not equally valuable across diffusion time: retaining the sampling updates while selectively reusing guidance can preserve generation quality with fewer denoiser evaluations. We introduce BATMoS (Budget Aware Temporal Mixture of Strategies), which routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser. A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.

papers.title: Exact Dynamic Scaling of Quantum Jump Statistics in Monitored Many-Body Systems
papers.abstract: Quantum measurement has opened a new frontier in nonequilibrium many-body physics, revealing striking phenomena such as measurement-induced entanglement transitions, whose experimental observation typically requires costly postselection. Quantum jump statistics offer another route to studying such measurement-induced many-body phenomena without postselection, motivating the search for universality in measurement outcomes themselves. In this Letter, we discover that fluctuation of the number of quantum jumps within a subsystem exhibits novel dynamic scaling, characterized by diffusive time scale and anomalous super-Poissonian system-size scaling that depend on the subsystem size in monitored many-body systems. For free fermions under continuous monitoring, we exactly determine the scaling exponent and the scaling function by deriving an exact finite-size solution of the Liouvillian autocorrelation function. We also analytically show that the dynamic scaling with the same scaling exponent and the scaling function even holds for interacting fermions in the limit of large measurement strength.
